speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the fact that no consensus or agreement was reached at the Law of the Sea Conference in Geneva and the next conference will not be held until March 29, 1976, in New York City, does the government plan on waiting for a general agreement that may not come within our lifetime or does it plan on taking unilateral action to protect Canadian offshore interests?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LAW OF THE SEA CONFERENCE-POSSIBILITY OF UNILATERAL ACTION TO PROTECT CANADIAN OFFSHORE RESOURCES IF CONFERENCE FAILS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think I answered this question last week, namely that there was delivered at the conference on Friday the single negotiating text which is now under study. In many aspects, it seems to meet the objectives of the Canadian government. However, it is still a negotiating text. It has to be negotiated at the next meeting. If it were possible to implement these provisions with respect to the fisheries immediately, one would be much more relaxed, but that is not possible. In the meantime, the government will appraise the situation and will consider among the possible options the prospect of unilateral action. However, that prospect has not yet been considered by the government as a whole.

subtopic: LAW OF THE SEA CONFERENCE-POSSIBILITY OF UNILATERAL ACTION TO PROTECT CANADIAN OFFSHORE RESOURCES IF CONFERENCE FAILS
speechtext: How long is the government willing to wait in hopes of getting general agreement? subtopic: LAW OF THE SEA CONFERENCE-POSSIBILITY OF UNILATERAL ACTION TO PROTECT CANADIAN OFFSHORE RESOURCES IF CONFERENCE FAILS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, obviously one of the possibilities is action in concert with a number of other countries. It concerns the number of diverse and ambivalent statements made in western Canada, both by telegram to the premier of Saskatchewan from the Prime Minister and statements made by the minister himself with regard to the Crowsnest Pass freight rates.
In view of the ambiguity of those statements, may I ask the minister whether it is his intention to assure the House and the country that the Crowsnest Pass rates will not be changed, diminished or monkeyed with between now and the next election?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE CROWSNEST PASS RATES WILL NOT BE CHANGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to repeat what in fact has been said in connection with the Crowsnest rates. Some little time ago, I did indicate at a meeting at Edmonton that there was some argument for a rate that better reflected real costs as between meat and grain in order to encourage the further processing of meat in Canada. I also indicated that that was in no way a proposal from the government but rather a matter that I was putting before the west as a matter of real interest to the west in so far as the further development of processing there is concerned. Some have since attempted to concern the farmers about this, because in my proposal I had indicated that it would have been my idea to maintain the benefits of the Crowsnest rates by transferring this sort of payment or assistance to the farmers more directly in some other fashion.
In order to ensure that there is no doubt at all in anybody's mind or no fear in anybody's mind about anything that this government is doing with regard to agriculture, I indicated that in my view the test whether such a change could be made was really dependent upon the will
(Mr. Marchand (Langelier).]
of the farmers themselves. I presume that the right hon. gentleman has his own conclusions about what that would mean at the present time. The fact of the matter is that it is above all clear that what the government is trying to do is to assure the best possible handling and transportation system that money can buy, the best possible income for the farmers, and the maximum number of farmers on our farms in the prairie provinces.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE CROWSNEST PASS RATES WILL NOT BE CHANGED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I suggest to the minister that the ambivalence has certainly been increased by that so-called statement. Let me ask him, why does he not say that there would be no interference or monkeying with the Crowsnest agreement rates? Why does he not say that simply and clearly, instead of a multitude of words chasing an idea that turns out to be as uncertain as the course of the government has been in this connection for months?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE CROWSNEST PASS RATES WILL NOT BE CHANGED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that if the hon. gentleman re-reads my statement he will understand that this government is always open to new ways to help the farmers even more. subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE CROWSNEST PASS RATES WILL NOT BE CHANGED

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE CROWSNEST PASS RATES WILL NOT BE CHANGED

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a result of our experience on Friday, when there was some confusion, there have been discussions through the usual channels and I should like to make some suggestions. I think I speak on behalf of the House leaders of the various parties with regard to our proceedings today and tomorrow. It is suggested that the
Business of Supply
Minister of Transport will not make a statement at the opening of the proceedings but that at 9.15 p.m. tomorrow he will be recognized for a 15 minute statement in summing up. A member of the opposition will then be recognized to conclude the two-day debate before the remaining votes are taken.
The minister's time in replying to questions is not to be counted as time taken by Liberal backbenchers; but on the other hand, speaking for this side of the House, we will not claim that Liberal backbenchers should have exactly the same time as all the opposition parties put together. Discussion, I suggest, should be divided into 15 minute units. A member may speak for ten minutes in developing questions, and the minister would have five minutes to respond or, alternatively, the minister and the member may engage in a 15 minute direct question and answer period. Of course, if a member so desires and does not expect or want a ministerial response, he may merely make a speech for that 15 minute period. Once a member of any party has used the 15 minute period, he will not be recognized again unless there are no other members of his party wishing to participate at that time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman has correctly stated the understanding we have reached. There will still be problems which Your Honour may have to contend with, but may I say in one or two sentences that have attempted to marry the old committee of supply to the other system under which we have been operating. Whether the result of that marriage will be a bastard or a child of some consequence, I do not know as yet; but it is going to throw some burden upon the Chair.
I just wish to make the point that in the old days committee of supply was all carried out on government time and ministers were in the position of having to be exceedingly nice to members of the opposition in order to get their estimates through. Unfortunately, those days are gone forever and they do not have to be nice to us any more-although I hope the Minister of Transport will be.
We are looking at a series of miniature, 15-minute capsule debates on certain issues and it is hoped that it will be realized that opposition days are being given up for this purpose. While I agree completely with the President of the Privy Council that government members who feel courageous enough, or have some issue to take up with the government, should have the right to do so, I hope that recognizing them will not mean that they will simply be here to take time away from the opposition.
Those are the points I wished to make. This experiment could be very successful and could bring us a long distance in recovering the ground we lost some years ago. I hope the Chair will take these things into consideration when deciding who is to be recognized and under what conditions.

Mr. Chairman, the President of the Privy Council has stated the terms of the agreement reached this morning among the House leaders. I do have one qualification that I will come to in a moment, Mr. Chairman, but it is not serious. I should like to make the point that we agreed this morning to try this procedure for these two days on the estimates of the Department of Transport, without committing ourselves to

May 12, 1975
Business of Supply
what we may do in the future. In other words, what we are trying to do is find a method that will work to the satisfaction of the committee in general. We are prepared to do our best to make this system work today and tomorrow and then decide where we will go from there.
There was one point in the statement of the President of the Privy Council that seemed to me to vary slightly from what we agreed to this morning. He said that if a member chooses to speak the full 15 minutes without putting any questions, he may do so. I think there was some concern this morning that a member might speak the full 15 minutes and not ask any questions, but make the kind of attack on the minister that would make him feel he should reply. Maybe we can cope with that if we come to it, but in any case the consensus was that we work on the basis of 15-minute units. We are prepared to try to make this plan work.

Mr. Chairman, I would really want to feel confident about the new suggestion put forward by the President of the Privy Council for a two day experience. Does such an agreement provide that the spokesmen of the various opposition parties in the House will have the opportunity to talk in turn or if this is left to the discretion of the Chair? I would want to receive such an assurance before we start our proceedings.

Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to see that there was further consideration of this matter. I was one of the members on this side of the House on Friday who was unhappy with the procedure. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that your ruling seems to be absolutely in line with what has been suggested today. Unfortunately, as time goes by in a day, different Chairmen chair the committee who do not know what went on previously and a misunderstanding develops. I would hope that if a member speaks for, say, five minutes and then puts questions, provided there is time left in his or her allotted time the minister will answer the questions if he can, or at least take them as notice, and do so right after the member has spoken.
I appreciate that we are all members of parliament and as such are responsible for curbing expenditures. The point that is being made by House leaders today is a good one, in that this is a unique responsibility of the opposition. We are trying to pry information out of the government. I have sat on the back benches of the government and I know that sometimes it is of benefit to the government to hide information. I think that ought to be taken into consideration in these procedures.
There is one further point that I should like to leave with you, Mr. Chairman, and I am afraid I disagree with my House leader on this. I hope that when we bring back the estimates into the House in this fashion, we will have not only the same privilege that we had in the past but the power that we had at that time. In the past we would tell a minister that the estimates would not pass until we got the information. All they do now is put up their collars and let the blizzard blow; when the blizzard is over, we

have no information. That is what we complained about on Friday.
I want to say, sir-I know I am not supposed to mention your ruling-that you were most fair and just under all the circumstances on Friday.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if this ruling, understanding or agreement among the parties takes into consideration the rights of members of parliament who are not members of parties?

speechtext: The committee has heard the suggestion of the President of the Privy Council. Is it agreed that today and tomorrow this will be the procedure adopted by the committee?

Mr. Chairman, in starting this two-day debate on the estimates of the Department of Transport, I hope we will be able to deal with questions at the time they are asked. I think this is far more pertinent and more helpful to the committee and to the member involved.
I should like to begin by saying that in the time this government has been in office, since 1972, the Department of Transport has not shown much in the way of results, in light of the election promises made at that time. When we look at the estimates we see a sizeable increase in all areas of expenditure of the department. I am going to deal with vote A, but before I do I should like to outline some of the election promises and try to show that almost none has been implemented. I think this is important in view of the fact that this House is going to be voting a large amount of money to the department.
In May, 1974, the Prime Minister stated that Air Canada was going to build major new facilities in Winnipeg at an estimated cost of $12 million, which would create 800 new jobs. The Prime Minister also said that Air Canada would discuss with the western provinces the establishment of a regional network of air services to serve small and isolated communities and create more employment. Another promise was for a STOL service to link Winnipeg, Brandon, Dauphin, Yorkton and Saskatoon.
On June 12, in Edmonton, the Prime Minister announced that if elected, his government would revise freight rates, set up a Crown corporation to supply boxcars, and improve the ports of Prince Rupert and Vancouver. That is another election promise that has not been carried out.
On June 17, in Toronto, the Prime Minister announced a $270 million program to aid public transit. To my knowledge, the government has not yet come up with anything positive on that program. The Prime Minister said on that occasion that a Liberal government would pay 100 per cent
May 12, 1975

of the cost of Canadian-made commuter vehicles and 50 per cent of the cost of platforms and stations. I could go on and on about the various promises made at that time, Mr. Chairman, but I am only trying to set the stage. In this debate we hope the minister will give the House of Commons the fullest information on the programs of the Department of Transport and the direction it will be taking in the future.
My first question to the minister concerns the headquarters of the department. According to the estimates, in the period 1975-76 over 1974-75 there is a 39 per cent increase in expenditures, which I feel is scandalous. I note that with respect to the 16.1 per cent increase in authorized man-years in 1974-75, part of the increase is attributed to improvements in public relations. Again, in 1975-76 a further 12.7 per cent increase in man-years authorized is to meet the growing demand for support in public relations. The information budget has increased from an actual expenditure of $48,000 in 1973-74 to an expenditure of some $1,687,000 in 1975-76. My question to the minister is this: From whom is there a growing demand for support in public relations? From where is that demand coming? Is it coming from the people of Canada? Apparently it takes 35 times more money to tell people this year that transportation is in a mess than it did two years ago. I ask the minister to explain the departmental figures concerning public relations.

Mr. Chairman, I will not answer all the statements which have been made, many of which are strictly political. The department has accomplished many things, and I will have the opportunity before this debate ends to tell the committee what the department has done in the west, with the agreement of the ministers of transport of the western provinces. I cannot ask the hon. gentleman to talk about Prince Rupert and the kind of agreement that we made with British Columbia about the development of northern B.C., about the development of Churchill or about the agreement reached with Manitoba, the maritimes, and so on. I will not take up the time of the committee with these matters; I know the hon. gentleman wants to gain some political credits in being strictly critical. This is what he is supposed to do and I am not going to interfere with that.
Of course, the total amount set aside for employees has increased considerably. We must take into account the training centre to be established in Cornwall, which will cost about $8 million. In addition, we must consider the new policy we are elaborating. I hope this will be ready soon. If the hon. gentleman scrutinizes the department's work objectively, he will agree that the number of hours spent in formulating the new policy justifies the differentials he alluded to. I do not know how much time I am to be allowed for answering.
The Chairman will tell you, never fear.

I do not intend to let the
hon. member speak and then not answer him. I am not like that. The man-years allotment for the transportation task force has been increased by about 101 man-years. In addition, there has been an increase in the number of
Business of Supply
employees in the minister's and the deputy minister's offices. The number of people employed in the information bureau-I think that is the right term-has been increased. In addition, there is an increase of 15 persons employed in the public affairs part of the department.
There are increases in the transport training institute, in those connected with the bilingualism program, in the computer service, in administration and in the general category. One must also include the central registry, the financial service, financial planning, operational revenue, material management, micrographics, and so on. In these areas you will find increases in man-years allowed. These employees are not political creatures; they are civil servants working for the government.

Mr. Chairman, I am not suggesting that the percentage of increase indicates any political hanky-panky; nevertheless, I think the figures justify our asking where the Canadian taxpayers' money is being spent. I suggest that we shall resolve the political aspect tomorrow night after 9.45 p.m. The minister suggested that the new policy will come forward soon. Can he be more specific? I understand that it has to do with modes of transportation involving roads, water, and so on. Can he say specifically when this new policy will be made known? Also, will he assure the committee that when the new policy is made known or comes forward, the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications will be able to review it before it is actually put into operation? I think the minister said this would be done.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has raised an important question. I remember the promise I made last year that I would discuss this policy with the standing committee of the House, and I intend to do so. First, I must have the approval of my colleagues. This is a government matter and I will discuss it in the near future with my colleagues. As soon as I have cabinet approval, I will be happy to discuss all aspects of transportation policy with the standing committee.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister another question? Another part of the 16.1 per cent increase in authorized man-years in 1974-75 is attributed to improvements in transportation policy. In 1975-76, part of 27 additional man-years is to be allocated, according to the explanation, to strengthening or developing the planning policy development functions: that is the way the matter is described. My question is this: What results has this increase produced so far? Also, if the policy development and planning development functions have been as heavily strengthened as is apparent from the estimates, why has the budget for professional and special services increased by 332 per cent since 1972-73? I suggest that the allocation in the 1972-73 budget was in the neighbourhood of $613,000; in the 1975-76 budget the amount allowed is in the neighbourhood of $2,652,000. Can the minister answer my question?

Mr. Chairman, I will try to answer the hon. member's first question and to get the figures from those who help me in order to answer the second question. I do not carry these figures in my head. To answer the hon. member's first question, let me tell

May 12, 1975
Business of Supply
him that the elaboration of the new policy was hard work. We established an important task force composed of people who know something about transportation. Of course, when I talk about policy I am talking about the general philosophy of transportation in Canada.
That policy must be acted on; we must do something concrete. It is not good enough to say that transportation in Canada should be an instrument of national development; to say we agree. But what do you mean by that? Who will have to work on programs and who will have to work on projects? We know that this task force will keep on for the rest of the year, and probably in 1976 in order that we will not only have a policy but programs and projects which correspond to this philosophy.
With regard to the other point, if the hon. member will wait a second, I will try to find out the information. I am told it has to do with the Cornwall institute. They have divided the cost of the building with the cost of the professional fees which are paid to architects, engineers, designers, and so on; that is the explanation for that amount.
Mr. Chairman-

speechtext: Order, please. Under the terms of the arrangement agreed to, the time of the hon. member for Lisgar has expired.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to use the time allotted to me at this juncture to put questions to the minister on three different subjects. They are not related to each other, so I will put one question, get the minister's answer, move on to the second, and so on.
As the minister will recall, during May and June of 1974-I will not say what was going on then because I do not want this to be that kind of a question-a good deal was said about urban renewal. The things that were being said under that heading included relocation of railway tracks in some or our cities and the development of new methods of transportation in our urban areas. Can the minister tell us what has happened, or what is happening to plans or projects that were in mind when those statements were made to the Canadian people in May and June of last year?

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member knows, transportation in urban areas is outside the jurisdiction of the federal government. However, we offered to co-operate with the provinces and municipalities in order to improve the transportation systems in large and medium sized cities. We cannot act on our own initiative; we had to meet with the provinces. We did that in order to determine how the problems could be solved.
I met with representatives of the British Columbia government and representatives of the city of Vancouver to see how we should proceed with regard to a better urban transportation system. This was also done in Winnipeg, Toronto and Quebec. We are now working with the provinces and the municipalities. This must necessarily be done by co-operation: we cannot impose our way of doing

things. For example, we cannot provide a commuter service without the co-operation of the province. We made an agreement for a commuter service from Richmond Hill, Ontario, to Toronto. The agreement is for $10 million. The service will be fed by all modes of transportation. People will be able to get to the heart of Toronto without having to wait many hours. This will avoid having to use thousands of cars which not only pollute but paralyse the city of Toronto. Therefore, we are working on this mainly with the minister of urban affairs. Everything is on the tracks, so to speak. I hope to see more achievements in the near future than have been seen up until this time.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the realism of the minister in referring to the necessity of co-operation between this government and the provincial governments and, in turn, with the municipalities. He will forgive me, I am sure, if I remind him that that was not quite the way it was given to the country last May and June. We were given great dreams of how our cities were going to be improved if the election went a certain way. However, we were aware of what was happening then. I am glad to know that at least something is being done.
The minister gave a bit of detail about the discussions relating to Toronto. Does he have at his fingertips any of the details relating to discussions involving Winnipeg?
I am sorry, I did not hear the last part.
I asked if the minister has any of the details regarding Winnipeg, similar to the details he has given about Toronto.

Mr. Chairman, there was a special study in Winnipeg. The problem is how to implement it. In the meantime, this House has passed the Railway Relocation Act. This was needed before we could do anything about the reform of urban transportation because we did not have the necessary money. We now have that instrument and we can work with the provinces and municipalities, not everywhere at the same time but according to our means. We intend to do that. We are ready to do this in Winnipeg because of the studies that have been made. As far as dreams are concerned, there is something I know. I am sure the hon. member shares my view. Anything that has been done in this world started with a dream. Mr. Woodsworth was a dreamer, a very nice dreamer.

Mr. Chairman, the minister in one of his better moments is trying to silence me. He makes it difficult for me to say that I am still aware of the difference between the things that were said last May and June about how quickly these things would happen if only the country would elect a Liberal government. I am glad to know the minister can say that something is being done. I hope he will turn these dreams into reality and we will not have to be given dreams all over again at the time of the next election.
My second question has to do with Air Canada. I will not steal the thunder of the hon. member for Central Nova. I want to deal with one specific problem and I shall
May 12, 1975

give one specific example of the problem. I have in mind Air Canada's labour relations. Is there not something the minister can do to persuade this Crown corporation, of which we in this House are very proud, to do something to get over the bad record that it is developing? The particular case in point that I wish to cite is that of the employees of the Air Canada finance branch at Winnipeg. Unhappy misunderstandings have persisted there for months. Perhaps by now it is a couple of years. I hope this is concerning the minister and that he can tell us what he is going to do about it.

Of course I am concerned about this problem; I would like to see labour relations working very well. Apparently there are some grievances in Winnipeg. One of the reasons, I presume, why so many of the things that came out through Winnipeg is that the people there were not satisfied with the way certain things were being done. This led to the inquiry which we instituted and which is now going on. I do not think it would be fair for Air Canada or its employees to begin discussing this issue at the moment, however. I realize that the hon. member's question had to do with labour relations which are not the subject of the inquiry led by Mr. Justice Estey, but I believe the inquiry will probably reveal many of the things that are going on inside Air Canada and the report might be helpful in leading to better relations between Air Canada and its employees.

Apparently the minister saw the look of puzzlement on my face when he referred to the inquiry which is taking place and intimated it would touch on the labour situation. I wondered if he was telling me that Mr. Justice Estey is looking into this aspect. If that is not the case, is there any other inquiry which can do so? Or is he saying that as a result of Mr. Justice Estey's inquiry, Air Canada will be put on its toes and realize it must patch up its labour relations in the same way as we hope it will patch up its financial affairs?

Even if there is no direct relationship between the grievances which have been expressed and the financial anomalies of Air Canada, there is no doubt the latter situation has some bearing upon the relationship between the group in Winnipeg and the headquarters in Montreal. Even if it is not a matter of collective bargaining, there is no doubt in my mind that some people are not satisfied with the way things are going. This creates unrest; it creates a bad atmosphere. If this were cleared up it would probably be easier to establish a better relationship within the organization.

If I share the minister's view, that means he shares mine. I hope he will pursue this matter with vigour. I have one other question, and if I gave the minister ten guesses he would guess it ten times. As we all know, a commission has been appointed by the Minister of Labour to deal with the whole question of railway pensions. Any questions relating directly to that inquiry should be directed to the Minister of Labour. But I shall narrow this issue down to that of Canadian National pensions. It is a question I have asked the minister during the question period. We have dealt
Business of Supply
with it on late shows. I find it difficult to jump too hard on the hon. gentleman because, again, I believe he agrees with me. But I am asking him to push as hard as he can with respect to this item.
It took a long time, and I mean a long time-decades-to get the CN to escalate the pensions of its retired employees. For decades, once CN workers had retired their pensions remained fixed throughout their lifetime. Four or five years ago we got those pensions escalated, but for about three years the escalation amounted to only 2 per cent a year and no more, no matter how much the cost of living went up. Last year, the CN improved the position by granting a 4 per cent escalation. But, Mr. Chairman, we are already in the month of May, 1975, and there has not yet been any escalation at all this year. I think the minister and I share the view that it is scandalous for the CN to ask its pensioners to wait all this time for a cost of living increase for 1975.
The excuse may be that the company is waiting for the Hall report. If so, that is not good enough. I am sure the report will not recommend anything less than the CNR and the CPR have been doing. Is there anything the minister can do to get the CN to come through, without further delay, with an escalation for 1975 in pensions of retired CN employees, either through his powers of persuasion or through his political clout? Since 10 per cent was the rate of escalation for the pensions of retired public servants, RCMP personnel, armed forces personnel, those on old age security and those receiving Canada Pension Plan benefits, that is what it ought to be with respect to CN pensions, certainly no less. This is my last question: Is there not something the minister can do to get Canadian National to be half decent to its retired employees?

The hon. gentleman talked to me about that last week, if my memory serves me well. I know there is a private bill on the order paper on this subject in the name of the hon. member for Levis. In the meantime, as I mentioned to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre-
Winnipeg "North" Centre.

Excuse me. I have never made any distinction as to that sort of thing. As I told the hon. member, I communicated with the chairman of the board of CN, making the representations he was making to me and with the same conviction, I think, as the hon. gentleman has displayed. The chairman of the board told me there was to be a meeting of the board on May 26 and that he understood very well our feelings here. Without giving a decision of the board-he is not authorized to do that-he did say he hoped we would be satisfied with the decision which would be taken. That is all I can say for the time being.

May I just say I shall question the minister about this on Tuesday, May
27?

May 12, 1975
Business of Supply

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad to have the opportunity to put some questions to the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand).
Since his announcement of a great reform in this House, it seems to me that it is still at the study stage. We are told that the study is going on, but I wonder whether, when it has been completed, the Minister of Transport will have more authority, generally, on air or railway transport. Even if personnel increases as the budget increases year after year, in our area, the higher the budget, the worse the service.
Strange enough, as the budget increases, we note personnel increases in more comfortable offices and, in the same way, decreases in maintenance, so that today I think there are four technocrats for one maintenance worker, who will see to the maintenance of railways or airports. This is the remark I wanted to convey to the Minister.
Every time we have elections, we can see countless airplanes flying in the sky of our constituency. We are given promises and, then, we are told that they were only election speeches. I think that it is kind of cheating the population of Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean. I know that the Minister is sometimes sincere. This afternoon I would like to put three or four questions to him. I would like him to answer directly, because he knows the needs of our area.
I would like to discuss airlines. He knows that the quality of air service in our area is presently at its lowest level ever. I do not know what are his plans for the future, but I would like to mention two or three problems and, particularly, the upgrading program of the Roberval Airport. I think it is the one he knows best. Does he still consider the Roberval Airport as the main one in our constituency? I would like to know what are his plans for this airport. In a moment, I will have another question to put about it. I would like to know his views on the Roberval Airport.

Mr. Chairman, I had a chance a couple of times to land at Roberval airport and for a small city that is located fairly far from the centre, it was indeed a rather wonderful experience to be able to land there in a jet. My hon. friend knows that Roberval strip quite well. In any case, as you know, the use of airports or the construction of landing and take-off runways is not simply a matter of government will. At the same time there must be people ready to use them and prepared to give the service.
It is not only a matter of saying: Let us build a landing strip, and let us wait and see, perhaps some people will use it. If we start developing that kind of philosophy I can assure you we might have to increase taxes, and I do not rely much on my hon. friend to convince the voters that it is a good thing.
In any case, there is the problem of traffic at an airport like Roberval. No doubt it is the most important in his riding but it is not the most important in the area because there is a bigger airport in Bagotville. Whether we like it or not, Mr. Speaker, the city of Chicoutimi is bigger than the city of Roberval, and to that I can do nothing.

As to the increase in costs, what happens to other services happens to airports too. It costs more to dig ditches today than a few years ago; it even takes a little longer and requires more people. Of course, we live in the same world. People used to work 60 hours a week, now they work 40, and I think my hon. colleague understands that quite well, even in his business.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. Minister for his reply but I would point out to him that when he said it was absolutely essential that municipalities do their share-and I think he realizes that himself-the city and parish of Roberval have done their big share and are still doing it today.
Now I want to ask him a question about another project. I think the hon. Minister has never been very clear nor very specific on that project that was requested by the northern towns, namely Dolbeau and St. Felicien, concerning the construction of another airport. I have here a recent reply dated April 14, 1975, about that project.
We would like an airport to serve northern towns. The Minister has already contacted those groups, but it would be what is called the Dolbeau-Saint-Felicien airport in Saint-Methode or an existing airport. Air navigation courses are given there. In the answer I have on hand it is mentioned that a final decision regarding the location of an airport in this area has not been made yet but that studies are made regarding harbour facilities.
I should like the hon. Minister to tell us what he thinks about that second request in the riding of Roberval?

Mr. Chairman, I think that has been very clearly announced in the speech from the throne and in the program of the Ministry of Transport. Communications between remote locations and the major centres of our country are very important. We wish to multiply the number of airports insofar as it is financially possible or insofar as they can be used enough to be profitable. Otherwise, we would have to build airports in each town, each village. I am not against it, but I shall tell you what it would cost and by how much taxes would have to be raised. In each area there must be a means of communication. First, the Saguenay area is well connected to the cities of Quebec and Montreal by the Bagotville airport; I think that nobody has to complain about it. In the Lac-Saint-Jean area, there is the Roberval airport which might be improved. A certain amount has been provided for it in our estimates. This year, I do not know what is the amount provided for municipal and small airports serving remote areas. When all the money has been spent, it is not possible to print more. In Roberval the runway is already built, it has only to be made practicable. It might be the best place to start and a small municipal airport might be built later in Dolbeau. All that will be achieved according to our means, and we believe the Dolbeau municipality is right to try and develop faster communications with communities in the area and the major centres in the province.

Mr. Chairman, my second question deals with another kind of transportation, railway transportation.
May 12, 1975

On several occasions, I blamed the government, and especially the Canadian National, because it was the only company operating in our area. Now, they are not only taking trains away, but also closing down stations. They removed the Dolbeau station clerk, and I got letters from Chicoutimi, Jonquiere and Iberville telling me stations had been closed down in that area too. I shall let hon. members for those areas say what they have to say about that. In my constituency, the clerk was removed, and tickets are no longer sold in Dolbeau, which is a serious situation in summer, because many workers leave from Dolbeau for the fruit and vegetable picking season. I think there is a considerable number of customers in Dolbeau during two or three months. But ticket sales have just been discontinued. This is what railway workers have been complaining about. They said: At least they should have done it in winter, not in summer, during peak traffic.
I wonder if the minister is aware of that.
The "express" service is also being discontinued. I do not know if it is cheaper, but "express" services are being contracted out. They go to Montreal to get "express" contracts. One was awarded in Abitibi, another one will soon be awarded to our area; I believe that very soon the Canadian National and all its bureaucrats will be driving their desks, with their only job being to give out contracts to private enterprise. I believe this is what is coming. As things are going now, even passengers will be farmed out.
I would like to know the minister's opinion on that, whether that is an improvement or whether it heralds the curtailment of our rail services?

Mr. Chairman, I suspect the hon. member is not completely aware of certain facts. They are quite the opposite from what he suggested. We are hearing numerous complaints about the Canadian National laying off employees. CP Rail does exactly the same thing. He says we are increasing the number of bureaucrats. On the contrary, I can assure him we are now reducing their numbers. They are bitterly complaining against it. I suggest the hon. member come to my office, where I can show him letters we are receiving exactly for this very reason that some are laid off.
We are now talking about a railroad and I think the hon. member will understand that it is not profitable to maintain a railroad on a year-round basis because the people in Dolbeau, Saint-Felicien, or elsewhere, use it only two months a year. If there is one area in the province where people use their car instead of the train to travel, it is in the Lac Saint-Jean area, and I know this area rather well since I lived there for many years. People like to have train service in case the roads are blocked or there are no other means of transportation. But this costs Canadian taxpayers a lot of money.
The problem in the Lac Saint-Jean area is the same as in Western Canada, where there are what are called "branch lines", which have not been used for years. Are we going to maintain them in the hope that one day we shall have customers who will board the train? I can give an example of this: there is at least one area in Canada which is costing us at least $6,000 a year for every passenger boarding the train.
