speechtext: Order, please. The time allotted to the hon. member for Roberval has now expired.

Mr. Chairman, it is sometimes said that living on Vancouver Island is reward enough in itself, but I wonder if I might refer to three areas of transportation in relation to Vancouver Island, ask a question on each and then sit down to allow the minister to reply. My first question relates to the fact that it is the present policy of the federal government and the minister's department to provide subsidies to ferries that operate interprovincially or that run from Canada to the United States.
The situation which exists in this regard in respect of the mainland of British Columbia and Vancouver Island deserves special attention because we do not have the Trans-Canada Highway connecting the mainland to the island, obviously, because of the Strait of Georgia. This is something about which the minister and myself can do nothing. However, because of the fact that earlier we did make provision for federal subsidies to provinces in respect of the Trans-Canada Highway from coast to coast, it should be relevant to consider some form of subsidy in respect of ferries. Perhaps this subsidy could be in the form of assistance in the construction of new ferries. A great number of people from other provinces in Canada use the existing ferry system and draw heavily upon those services to the people of British Columbia, particularly Vancouver Island, and for this reason I think we should look seriously at the idea of providing subsidies for this very important service between Vancouver Island and the mainland.

Mr. Chairman, we have been discussing this with the hon. member and the government of British Columbia for many months. We are trying to determine if it is possible to do this without creating a precedent that would, of course, cost the federal government hundreds of millions of dollars. If we decided to subsidize all intraprovincial ferries, the cost would be tremendous. We have departed from this policy and we have in many cases succeeded in eliminating all ferries which were operating within the limits of provinces.
In the case of British Columbia, we have been given some reasons for providing such a subsidy, probably the most important of which is the one referred to by the hon. member, that is, that the Trans-Canada Highway should really start in Victoria and continue from the mainland in Vancouver, maintaining the link from Vancouver Island to Newfoundland. Such a link should be part of the federal responsibility, and this is something we have been trying to achieve, but the hon. gentleman will understand that if we did this generally for ferries, then I do not know how we could avoid doing it in respect of bridges. The same argument would apply because they, too, form part of the Trans-Canada Highway. This is not something we are refusing to discuss and the hon. member can be assured that I am ready again to look into the situation.

The second matter I should like to refer to is one that affects the northern part of Vancouver Island and the cessation of barge services to the isolated

Business of Supply
communities there. This service has been cut off because of the sparsely inhabited area, yet the barges are the only means of transportation since there are no roads or railroads in that area. I believe there is a precedent in that the federal government does subsidize the cost of bringing freight to those isolated communities in northern Vancouver Island by a ship called the Yewchuk. Recently, the Sea Span Barge Company of Vancouver terminated services to these isolated communities because, as it claimed, the cost of stopping at these areas was higher than the charge for delivering the freight. In other words, it is an uneconomical endeavour in view of the capital investment involved in bringing freight to these communities.
Since there is a precedent in that we do provide a subsidy to some sort of freight services for other isolated communities, I would suggest that we should provide a considerable subsidy to the Sea Span Barge Company which has within the last few months stopped providing this service to many communities on northern Vancouver Island because it is not profitable.

Mr. Chairman, I come back to the argument I was advancing a few minutes ago. We are providing this kind of subsidy in the Northwest Territories because there is no provincial government there. We do it at this moment in Hudson Bay, for example, and the Arctic Ocean and through the Mackenzie River because those are territories where there is no provincial government.
Of course, we grant subsidies-and this might be a precedent-to the maritime provinces for intratransportation, partly by truck. To a certain extent this might be comparable to what we do in the Newfoundland coastal service which is within the limits of a province and to which we grant some subsidies. We can look at it again. We knew that private enterprise could not make money on it and would abandon this kind of service. We can either have some sort of agreement with the B.C. government or we can do it in the same way we are doing it in Newfoundland and the maritimes.

Mr. Chairman, one of the things that should be pointed out at present is that, surprisingly enough, in the northern two-thirds of Vancouver Island, including the point from Nanaimo north, we have fewer transportation facilities than there are in the Yukon. The Yukon is considered to be a fairly remote territory which does not have some of the amenities of life that we are supposed to have in the southern part of Canada. But I think it is very interesting to point out that in the northern two-thirds of Vancouver Island, beside the fact that there is absolutely no rail transportation, we have no roads apart from logging roads at present and our airports there are fairly restricted. Therefore, we have a definite problem.
I would like to ask the minister a general question. In view of the fact that in my opinion this is a situation for which one can blame the federal, the provincial or the municipal government, would it not be appropriate, in view of the abysmal lack of transportation in our area, for a transport committee inquiry to be held regarding what

May 12, 1975
we could do and what co-operation we could get from the various levels of government in order to make that area inhabitable? We have resources in that part of the Island, including copper and other minerals, and we have a tremendous forest industry in the area, but we are unable to keep people up there because of the isolation and lack of means of communication such as railroads, radio and television.
To be quite honest, I will do anything in my power to bring this matter to the attention of the minister as well as the provincial government. In my opinion, this area has been neglected for many years. I will not go into the reasons it has been neglected, but let us start with the assumption that there is need for an inquiry into how we can bring that area, so full of potential, into production so we can increase the benefits from the area and keep families and communities together, instead of having people come up there for several months in order to earn enough money to go back to the large cities.
Could an inquiry be held so that at some time in the future we could consider providing various modes of transportation such as ferries, highways, air transportation, and so on, and so we could provide a service for the people in this area who have been crying for help from the various governments for many years?

In order to answer this question properly I would have to reveal a part of the new policy which we are designing. One of the points that we have studied in depth is the accessibility of certain communities because, of course, Canada is not the same everywhere, as the hon. member knows. Southern Ontario is different from northern Ontario which, again, is different from the Northwest Territories or the lower St. Lawrence. We will have to find formulas so that all these people can feel they are Canadians and have means of communicating with the main centres of Canada. This is something we are looking into.
We were speaking about subsidies a few minutes ago. Let me state that so far as British Columbia is concerned, right now we are giving over $700,000 to Vancouver and the northern ports, and for the service on the west coast of Vancouver Island-this is inside the province-we pay more than $168,000 through the CTC. So we are already doing something in this area. The problem which the hon. member raised, however, is a practical one of the accessibility of isolated communities. We have this problem not only on Vancouver Island but in many places in the north. Almost the whole of the northern portions of the provinces are in the same situation: they can hardly communicate with the south. The problem is one of isolation.
This is not the time to brag about it.
This is a problem to which we will pay much attention.

I can understand that the problem occurs in the northern parts of our Canadian provinces, but I think it should be brought to the attention of the minister that we run into a special problem: this area is not even in the north, in the geographical sense. The problem is merely in the fact that we have mountains, fiords and inlets which tend to break up the communication links
May 12, 1975

that we could have there. The difficulty of the problem lies not only in the inaccessibility of certain communities but in the cost of putting in services, which is bound to be very high.
The only redeeming feature-and one has to be practical in looking at these things-is the fact that there is tremendous potential in the area in respect of lumber, fishing and mining. This is a vicious circle, because population is needed there before the services can be provided. However, in order to get the people there, we need services to begin with. We seem to have been going around in circles for many years.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but the time allotted to him has expired.

Mr. Chairman, I hope to have the opportunity to discuss for a few moments with the minister two or three topics related to Air Canada, and I shall do everything I can to avoid impinging on any areas of the inquiry being conducted by Mr. Justice Estey. However, I would like to say to the minister that I had the opportunity to attend the hearings briefly, and I can assure him that he can be most satisfied and proud of the way in which the hearings are being carried out. Certainly, I was impressed with the way in which the hearings are conducted, the calibre of counsel, and all other procedures.
Perhaps at the end of my brief remarks the minister will deal with the points I have raised. First, I would like to ask him to what extent he has been kept informed, and to what extent he feels it is proper for him to be kept informed on an ongoing basis of the management and policy decisions of Air Canada. Does he receive, for example, from time to time, regular reports from the chairman and chief executive officer and copies of the minutes of meetings of the executive committee of Air Canada? Consequently, does he make some input himself into certain basic policy decisions of our national air carrier?
I would also like to discuss briefly the proposed reorganization of Air Canada's southern and United States region where it is contemplated that the southern region, comprised of some sovereign countries in the Caribbean, will be amalgamated with the United States region and the office of the United States region, which is now in Los Angeles, moved to 600 Madison Avenue, New York, with a target date as I understand it of approximately August 1 this year. I suggest that this, in effect, makes southern locations located in the central regions since 1971 part of the United States region which will be called the United States and southern region.
Without going into the matter in great detail, I wonder if the Minister could say whether he is aware of the implications of what is being done, and is he aware that reports and submissions have been made by officials of the Department of External Affairs to executives of Air Canada conveying opposition felt by some Caribbean countries at being lumped in with the United States? I am informed that these nations feel a greater affinity toward Canada than the United States, and that there is a feeling special relationships could be lost if they must be con-
Business of Supply
sidered as part of the United States rather than having their own special relationship with Air Canada, our national air carrier.
Before the minister answers I would like to suggest, also, that besides this possibly being counterproductive as far as efforts by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of External Affairs are concerned with respect to their aims in the Caribbean area in extending Canada's good offices and sphere of influence, there is also the case of businessmen in what is now the southern region having to change their procedures in dealing directly with Canada, since I suggest that if the region is amalgamated according to the proposed plan, businessmen may have to obtain a rate to Canada through the New York office rather than dealing directly with a Canadian centre. This could be objectionable, and although I am not suggesting to the minister that this proposed reorganization is necessarily bad, I wonder if he is aware of all the various consequences of it and whether it could be a regressive step, taking into account the whole picture. I hope the minister will carefully consider this question and deal with it, if not today then quite soon.
Another topic I would like to discuss is related to remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre about labour-management relations. I have enormous respect for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and I would also like to go on record as saying that it is not my purpose, and I am sure it is not the purpose of any member, to denigrate, hurt or undermine Air Canada but to try to improve this great institution of which we are all proud. However, I am wondering about the cost factors and some of the problems of Canada's image involved in the strike in Paris. There was also a problem in New York, as the minister knows, with the IAM people walking out a few days ago. It seems to me that the contracting out procedures Air Canada is taking might merit some personal review by the minister.
I would also like to know if we could have some statistics on the cost of this Paris strike because, as I understand it, the regular Air Canada fare from Toronto to Paris is $328. Because of the strike in Paris, it is necessary to take passengers from Toronto to London, England. That fare, at $315, is somewhat cheaper, but to carry on to Paris there is an additional sector fare of approximately $57. The airline, of course, is responsible and must absorb the cost of approximately $44 because it is an involuntary re-routing, using airline parlance.
It has also come to my attention that some passengers who would have boarded in Montreal for Paris must be taken to Toronto. The fare is another $37 for these passengers. So all in all, I suggest that considerable financial losses are taking place because of this contingency with which our airline must cope. The image of Air Canada in France must be considered. There are certain French laws, as the minister well knows, which have to be taken into consideration in determining the future of these employees of Air Canada whose services are apparently no longer needed.
In concluding my remarks, I would like to say sincerely to the minister that, being on the opposition side, it is most difficult for us and for me to obtain the type of hard, accurate information which is necessary to suggest

May 12, 1975
Business of Supply
changes or investigations. In the past, I have tried to be reasonably accurate with information I have given. I would now like to bring to the attention of the minister a situation which may exist-this is perhaps one of the most interesting parts, at least for me-where I have reason to think it would be a good idea if he would check to see what the relationship is regarding certain management consultant firms or personnel placement firms which deal with Air Canada, and supply or refer executives to this company.
As I understand it, it is the practice of the trade-at least, it has taken place in the past-that there is a fairly generous finder's fee involved when a personnel placement agency supplies an executive to Air Canada say at a salary of $40,000 per year. If the executive stays with the company for over six months, Air Canada is obligated to pay to the personnel placement agency half of the executive's salary for the first year, as a finder's fee, which, on the basis of the example of $40,000, would amount to $20,000.
I have reason to believe that a situation exists where in at least one case, and perhaps in others, a man who was vice-president and general manager of one of these finding bureaux, if I may use that term, arranged to have himself placed with Air Canada and worked there long enough that the firm which placed him qualified for the finder's fee, which was quite substantial because he was a fairly highly paid executive. During this time, the unusual part of the arrangement may well have been that he perhaps never really divested himself of his former interest and former position with the agency where he used to work which placed executives with Air Canada. If this type of situation does exist, it seems, to my comparatively untutored reasoning, that there could be a problem. I do not know how widespread it is. I have only heard of this particular instance.
There is another side to this situation which may be even more unusual than the one I have stated, and this is that one of the vice-presidents of Air Canada has a direct or indirect relationship with this management consultant firm. If that is the case, the minister can see the unusual problem involved. If, and I emphasize "if", this happens to be the case, I feel that the minister should be concerned. In checking into the relationships between management consulting firms of this type and Air Canada, perhaps the minister would begin by looking to see if that possibility exists with regard to the firm of John Hold Stethem-Claude Gareau Limited, of Montreal. There also is an Ontario wing of the company. If there is any substance to this, perhaps in the course of a few days the minister might make a report. If he requires more background information, I would certainly supply it to any of his officials.

Mr. Chairman, I can be more precise with regard to that relationship later on. Canadian National is the owner of Air Canada. Canadian National has representatives on the board, and so have we. What strikes me in the relationship between the federal government and its Crown corporation is that it is not the same type of relationship as exists with any of the other Crown corporations. It depends, I presume, on the minister or the government in power at any given time. I

remember that Mr. C. D. Howe, who was not a socialist, created four or five Crown corporations and probably depended upon-
Where is he, now that we need him?

We have a situation that is difficult to understand. For instance, the president of Northern Transportation Company is a member of Eldorado mines which is a Crown corporation. As president of the Northern Transportation Co. Ltd. he reports to me, while Eldorado mines reports to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. This is the way it was set up, and perhaps some day we can correct this.
We receive the minutes of the meetings of the board of directors of Air Canada-not of the executive committee but the reports of the board of directors. That is outside the control of the government; that is, the control that the government can exercise over the budget. Of course, Air Canada is more dependent on the CNR than it is on us. These are the things we have been looking into, and in future we will probably have a more normal kind of relationship.
As far as the vice-president who is involved in a placement is concerned, and whether there is a conflict of interest, I will make inquiries in the department and get the answer on that. Personally, I was not aware of that and I will be happy to look into it and give an answer before tomorrow night.

Madam Chairman, I want to deal with some of the matters touched on by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre concerning the programs of the government in aid to public transit in some of the larger urban areas. The question was put to the minister with regard to certain cities, and I should like to put the question in regard to the national capital region. It may be that I am putting the question to the wrong minister and, if so, I am sure I will be set straight.
I should like to know what program there is for the development of plans for other forms of mass transit in the national capital region, in the hope that the federal government might be able to take more initiative in this particular area for which it has more responsibility than it has in many other urban areas in Canada. I hope it will be possible for the federal government to do certain things in the national capital region that will be by way of demonstration projects to other urban communities across Canada to illustrate what is it possible to do in the way of innovation and things that are new. In this connection, I should like to know what measures the department is taking by way of encouragement in basic research in urban transit.

The city of Ottawa is on the same footing as all the other important cities in Canada. I do not have special responsibility as far as the national capital region is concerned. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs is in charge of the National Capital Commission, and I know that plans have been discussed by the city, the province of Quebec and the NCC. The Department of Transport is not involved at this stage but might
May 12, 1975

be later, as the province of Ontario might also become involved. I know they are working on all kinds of projects, but unfortunately I cannot enlighten my colleague about what is being done at this moment.

I appreciate the answer of the minister. I do not wish to press him on a matter which is not his responsibility, but I am interested in what he has to say as a senior member of cabinet and one who is experienced and knowledgeable in these matters. I wonder if one element that might bring forward something of special interest would be the money that the government is saving now in the national capital from the charges that are being made for parking facilities, which I support. There is a saving of perhaps $5 million a year to the government in this respect. I hope that the net effect will be to encourage the government to look to other measures that might assist because there is such a saving to it, in discouraging people from using private cars and to look with favour at alternative methods of getting to and from their employment.
In view of the special savings accruing to the government as a result of these policies, I hope the minister will confer with his colleagues to consider whether additional measures to encourage public transit can be undertaken.

Madam Chairman, I wonder if I might continue with the unhappy saga of passenger rail service in southwestern Ontario, a matter with which the minister is closely concerned and which has been raised repeatedly in this House since March or April, 1970. In order that the minister not be unnecessarily confused by other matters, such as urban transit around the city of Toronto, perhaps I should trace the history of the service, or lack of it, since 1970. In that year the CTC held public hearings as a result of a CNR application to discontinue certain trains. Permission for discontinuance of 400 miles of passenger service was given in November, 1970, in spite of a mountain of evidence of the necessity for the service.
During 1971, there was considerable debate in this House and considerable public uproar about the discontinuance of service. In the spring of 1972, the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications was charged with the responsibility of holding hearings throughout southwestern Ontario to determine the adequacy of passenger rail service. The committee visited London, Chatham, Stratford and Walkerton in the spring of 1972. The committee's report was published in June, 1972, and included a unanimous recommendation that the passenger service eliminated on November 1, 1970, be immediately reinstated.
In the twenty-ninth parliament a series of questions were asked, starting in April, 1973. There were motions, debates, petitions and groups which came to Ottawa. I remember that in the winter of 1972 or early spring of 1973 the warden of one of the counties affected went back to his locality and was reported in the Guelph Mercury of June 15, 1973, as saying:
Our brief was very well received and Mr. Marchand appeared to react in a most favourable way to our presentation. I believe I can say that after our talks I am optimistic about the future of our area and provision of proper transportation for its residents.
Business of Supply
That response was typical of the people who came to Ottawa and who talked to the minister, his parliamentary secretary or departmental officials. They always left Ottawa feeling optimistic. In mid-1973 the minister started talking about the CTC study and tri-level discussions, and emphasized the need to consult local people. In September, 1973, he agreed to release the CTC study around the first or second week of October. Nothing happened, Mr. Chairman. On November 20, 1973, Mr. Benson appeared in the standing committee along with the minister and said that the report might be ready by the end of November. He also mentioned a survey that was being taken by the CTC of some 12 families in the area affected.
On January 7, 1974, in reply to a question which I put to him in the House, the minister said that he had received the CTC report, it had to be distributed to all interested parties and that it was to be studied soon at a tri-level conference. I believe that everyone took tri-level to mean federal, provincial and municipal. On January 8, the next day, it was determined that the report had not been made available to members of parliament, provincial representatives, municipal officers and the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. On January 9, 1974, we were still waiting for the third portion of the report consisting of the survey, Gallup poll or whatever one may call it.
Finally, in 1974, parts I and II were tabled. Part III, received by the minister well over one year ago, has never been tabled despite requests to that effect. During 1974, the CNR continued to dispose of its railway stations in southwestern Ontario and continues to do so to this day. In October, 1974, the minister stated that the matter was still under study with Ontario and there was no further reference to tri-level conferences or consultations with municipal officials or others directly affected by this loss of service. On October 23, 1974, during debate on the Treasury Board estimates, an hon. member read the following portion of a letter dated October 9 and written by the minister's research assistant, as reworded on page 683 of Hansard:
Last year, the CTC's research branch carried out a thorough study of transportation services in the area and came to the conclusion that rail passenger services were not supportable by the population and that the preferred method of travel would be an improved rationalized bus service, a possible link to the existing main line passenger trains between London and Toronto.
That brings us up to date. May I now ask the minister a number of questions? First, has a tri-level conference ever been convened, as promised by the minister on January 7, 1974?

Madam Chairman, we held a tri-level conference in Toronto at which the urban community was represented by Mr. Rhodes, a member of the Legislative Assembly of Ontario. There were other meetings in Ottawa, on this matter, with the provincial minister responsible for roads. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs is trying to institute the tri-level conference system right across Canada. This is a long process as some provinces are reluctant to include municipalities in an organization which includes provincial and federal governments. There are some difficulties of adjustment. We

May 12, 1975
Business of Supply
have met, probably four of five times with the government of Ontario in an attempt to resolve some problems which have existed since 1970 or 1972.

Madam Chairman, may I ask the minister why the third part of the CTC study, referred to as the survey, Gallup poll or what have you, has never been made available to members of parliament, provincial representatives or municipal officials? Why has the minister refused, to date, to table that report? If he is not refusing, will he tell us when he intends to table it?
He knows nothing about it; he is conferring with his officials.
Please excuse me, Madam Chairman; I am looking for the report as well.
The CTC would not even give it to the minister.
Perhaps it has been lost somewhere in the mail.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Move for the production of papers.

Madam Chairman, before tabling the report we must have agreement of the government of Ontario. After we obtain that agreement we can table the report and make known the basis on which we reached agreement.

Madam Chairman, may I ask another question arising from that answer? Has the government of Ontario not completely repudiated the efficacy of that report and suggested that it is totally unsatisfactory? It was not satisfied with the questions asked, with those to whom questions were directed or with the responses demanded by the nature of the questions. In other words, has not the province of Ontario said to the Department of Transport, "This report is completely unacceptable"?

Madam Chairman, I am told the province does not like the report. We are still working on the problems which must be solved in southwestern Ontario. Of course, if the province does not accept the report and does not accept our efforts at co-operation, we will not table the report: what would be the purpose?

Madam Chairman, does the minister consider it acceptable for his department to operate on the basis of reports prepared by the CTC, when the CTC ordered the discontinuance of services in the first place? In other words, is the report of a body which is really sitting in judgment on its own decisions acceptable as a guide for future policy decisions the minister might make?

Madam Chairman, I suggest that the hon. member should read the speech I made in the House on a previous occasion. Do we want to change the law? The CTC is given wide powers, and I do not know how many inquiries the CTC is making at one time. They have the authority to do this, and most of the time they are not even under the obligation of communicating the results to me. That is the way matters stand, and this was

done with the acceptance of this House: many of us were here when we passed that law.
I do not blame anybody. We thought we were setting up a regulatory body which would prove useful. I think it is useful to have this regulatory body. The question is, can we take away from government the responsibility in this field? All I can say at present is this: it is just too bad, but they did not send me the report. They decided to hold an inquiry, but I did not ask for one. This is the way matters stand. If we want to change that state of affairs, we will have to make some suggestions to the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. minister, but according to the agreement made today, the time allotted to him has now expired.

Madam Chairman, may I direct several questions to the minister. Since the holding of the western economic opportunities conference in Calgary, a number of policy thrusts have been announced and agreed upon by the federal government, in particular the Ministry of Transport, and provinces of Canada, particularly western Canada. I wish to ask the minister when the government intends to implement the announcements made by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Justice in last year's election campaign. Specifically, I am referring to the minister's commitment to establish a passenger train corporation. What has happened to that corporation? When does the government intend to establish it? Also, has money been set aside in the present estimates for the corporation?

Madam Chairman, during the election campaign we said that if the passenger train system were not improved we would create a new corporation that would be given responsibility for operating passenger trains in Canada. The first thing I did after the election was to ask Mr. Sinclair and Mr. MacMillan to come to my office: I asked, "Are you interested in operating passenger trains, because you are losing money?" They both said they were very keenly interested in operating passenger trains.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: If the price was right.

Yes, that is what they told me. I asked what they intend to do about it. There is something new since then. We do not intend to stop there. We now have a turbo train which operates between Montreal and Toronto and another between Ottawa and Montreal. CP is ready to start the LRC train. They want to operate this between Ottawa and Montreal, but we are not sure that is the best thing to do. Our agency in Montreal, the Transportation Development Agency, is working on this aspect of the problem.
If we cannot get a satisfactory decision from the railways, we will create this corporation. This has not been put aside. It is a right that we reserve and which will be exercised if the railways keep this attitude of not operating their services in the field of passenger trains, prefer-
May 12, 1975

ring to use old cars rather than renewing their rolling stock.

Other than the turbo train and the LRC experiment, neither railroad has placed any orders for new equipment. They have not extended any money to prove their so-called interest in passenger train service. Does the minister take that as any kind of sign that he should now move on a publicly-owned passenger train service?

Madam Chairman, I do not think that would be reasonable. We want to have a new, progressive policy in that field. We want the railways to follow this policy. However, it is difficult to ask them to follow a policy which is not yet known. This is why it is urgent that there be this policy. It must be approved by cabinet and the House. If the railways then do not want to do that, it will be just too bad; we will do it ourselves.

The minister has had 12 months to say that to them. I will now refer to another specific item in the Liberal Party's election program commitment-a freight car leasing corporation. Aside from the hopper cars that we all know about, since World War 11 the railroads have been short of freight cars, refrigerator cars, stock cars and gondola cars; there is no denying that. Is there anything about this in the estimates? What is the government policy to carry out a commitment they made in June and July last year with regard to a freight car leasing corporation?

Madam Chairman, the hon. member's questions are all related to the policy on which we have been working and which we want to announce. After that, the hon. member will be justified in saying we have forgotten a part of what we had intended to do. Of course, the situation this year is not the same as last year when we had a shortage of not only hopper cars but lumber cars and even box cars. There has been no such shortage this year. Of course, the economic situation is different. We have instituted a monitoring system which has helped us to a certain extent in attaining better productivity from our cars. The hon. member's question concerns something which is supposed to be integrated in the general policy we are about to produce.

I will move to another specific item in the commitments made by the government in June and July of last year and repeated in the communique issued on February 24 as a result of the conference in Calgary between the minister and his counterparts in the western provinces. It has to do with the freight rate structure. The minister and his counterparts said the principles on which they were going to act, led by the Minister of Transport, included rate groupings, a reduction of horizontal increases, maximum rate restrictions and the anomalies in the long haul-short haul of raw and finished products.
These anomalies have been compounded twice in the past six months. As a result of the public statements made by the presidents of both railroads, I understand they will be compounded. I remind the minister that the spread between shipping live cattle and dressed beef from Saskatoon to Montreal, Ottawa or Toronto, used to be 91 cents a hundredweight more for dressed beef than live cattle: it now costs $1.17 more a hundredweight. Since January 1,
Business of Supply
the spread has increased by 26 cents a hundredweight. That flies in the face of the communique of February 24 with regard to anomalies between raw and finished products. The packing industry in western Canada is in great difficulty.
The minister has allowed, in violation of the February 24 communique, a horizontal increase. That is violation number one of four items in the communique. Second, there is a violation of item number 4 in that communique with regard to the anomalies between raw and finished products. What is the minister going to do about that? What legislation does he have to give the authority? Are we going to get it? What is in the estimates concerning the commitments that were made by the Liberal Party during the election compaign and the February 24 communique?

Madam Chairman, we never said, and never will say, unless the policy of this government changes, that there will not be increases in rates in Canada. The western ministers and I spoke about rate grouping and horizontal increases; that is true. We also talked about a few other matters. We will stick to the policy we agreed to with the western ministers. New across the board increases which concern mainly what are called the class rates, and dont't forget this is only 4 per cent of the revenues of the railways-
That has nothing to do with it.

It has something to do with it. If we look at the items and how they are broken down, we see all the categories with all rates increased, and it is not an across the board increase. The hon. member knows what an across the board increase is. Anyone connected with the labour movement knows that it means the same amount for everyone. The railways have not done that. Even if all the rates have been touched, the increases have still been selective. Therefore, we need to have the same definition for what across the board means and what actually happened. As far as the rest is concerned, we are still working with the western ministers so that the policy that was announced is implemented.

There is another item which has been hanging fire for four years or so. If the cabinet has made a decision on it lately, I regret my ignorance. I refer to the rates on rapeseed oil and rapeseed products. The western provinces appealed a decision of the Canadian Transport Commission in March of 1974. Has the cabinet made a decision yet and, if so, what was the nature of that decision? This matter goes back to a legal dispute between the shippers and the railways, the provinces supporting the producers and shippers. An appeal was made to the cabinet. What happened?

We are waiting for a supplementary report from the CTC and we have asked that this report should be made available as soon as possible. The question of rapeseed rates is a very complicated one because it is related, to a certain extent, to the Crowsnest pass rate system. We have to judge what the impact is likely to be and, of course, we take all the time we need in order to protect the farmers of the west. We are expecting

May 12, 1975
Business of Supply
this report, but I can tell the hon. member personally that this is one of the most complicated problems which has ever come to my attention in the Ministry of Transport.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The time allotted to the hon. member has expired. Before recognizing the hon. member for Hastings, I should like to inform the committee of the questions to be raised tonight at the time of the adjournment. They are as follows: the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark)-Health-Asbestos levels in Lake Superior; the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall)-Fisheries-Exclusion of some areas of Newfoundland from compensation program; the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dins-dale)-Air Transport-Service for southwestern Manitoba and southeastern Saskatchewan.

Madam Chairman, there are so many questions which could be asked during the time available for questioning the minister that it baffles the mind, especially as so few answers are apt to be given; it has been extremely difficult to get information from the minister during the year. During the first session of this parliament some 346 questions were directed to the hon. gentleman or, in his absence, to the parliamentary secretary or, once in a while, to the acting minister of transport. This figure does not include the number of questions on the order paper or questions about transport directed to other ministers from time to time. Of those 346 questions, about one-third concerned railways-half of those on freight rates-and approximately one-third related to air transport. A large number of the latter concerned Air Canada; and there were, of course, a large number of questions lately on the popular subject of dredging.
However, we are not receiving answers to these questions. I have directed a good many questions to the minister, but most of the time we get from him a statement that the subject is under study, that he will inquire into it. In reply to one question which I directed to the hon. gentleman some time ago, I got the one word, "Soon". That was about a month and a half ago and I have received no further information since then.
This being a committee of supply, questions ought rightfully to be addressed, I suppose, to the increase which has taken place in the department's budget. My hon. friend from Lisgar asked a number of questions with regard to public relations. I recall asking similar questions in the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications and these, in turn, prompted me to make further inquiries. I will read through some of the questions and then give the minister a chance to answer them.
The increase in the cost and size of the department has, frankly, shocked me even against the current background of inflation. For example, the budget for the headquarters of this department has increased in three years by 108 per cent. Madam Chairman, this bears no relation to any increase in costs that we have seen or any indices which are available to us, which leads me to believe that these increases are actually leading inflation, not following it, and that they are the root cause of inflation in many areas.
I recall being involved in a discussion regarding one specific area of marine transportation. I might say I admire the minister's frank answers to certain questions

even when such answers might obviously be somewhat embarrassing. I asked a question concerning marine transportation and I remarked there had been a 32 per cent increase authorized in man hours during 1975. I was curious how all these people could be employed-whether they were being used for cannon fodder or something like that. We were given to understand that studies were going on concerning two different types of ice-breakers. The minister himself brought out the fact that the department was actually engaged in studies concerning three different types of ice-breakers. I admire his frankness, but surely it would be possible to carry out one study directed at three types or ice-breakers rather than three studies of ice-breakers.
I am not being critical of individuals, but one day I did a rough calculation of the number of staff on hand during the committee hearings and found they outnumbered the members supporting the government on the committee, they outnumbered the members of the opposition, they outnumbered the spectators and they outnumbered the committee staff. My estimate was that it would cost between $10,000 and $15,000 to pay the salaries of the staff present during the hearings of that one committee. One of my hon. friend points out that they almost outnumber us in the chamber this afternoon. It is gratifying to see them here, in a sense, but my point is that with so many members of the staff available we should be able to get answers to some of the questions we ask.
In reply to one of the questions we asked in connection with transportation safety, the answer was given us in a document prepared by the Canadian Transport Commission. I know the minister does not feel that this commission comes under his authority, but reference was made in that reply to setting out a conceptual model for defining the socially optimal level of safety. Madam Chairman, what in heaven's name is a conceptual model for defining the socially optimal of safety? As I have said before in this chamber, I am just a huckleberry from Hastings county. But does the minister really know what that is? Apparently it is a tool. It says here it is an important tool. I don't know what kind of tool it is, but I get a little upset about the use of that kind of language, considering that a number of people we have here should be able to speak English.
With the range of questions open to us, I know I could go on for two hours without running out of questions. However, I want to put a few specific questions to the minister, in the time I have left, regarding the amount spent on consultants by his department. Again I hark back to the very large staff the department has. I remember at one time I facetiously asked the deputy minister whether he had brought the whole department with him, but I was assured that he had brought only a very small portion along. I have had individual dealings with members of the staff and there is no question that they have some very talented people. But with this wealth of talent, why do we make extensive use of consultants?
I should like to ask the minister to be good enough to give me an answer in respect to some of these examples. The first is a firm from New York city, John J. McMullen Associates, on whom we spent $46,000 to design a flame
May 12, 1975

stabilization system for a railcar carrier. Another firm, R. L. Banks and Associates, of Washington, D.C., received a contract for $260,000 to study railway pricing methods and the effect that such methods have upon national and regional economics in Canada. Then a firm called Bruce Mallen and Associates-I like this example particularly- received a contract for $27,500 to undertake up to 700 interviews relating to motivational aspects of the private industry in Canada and provide information in tabulated form. Once again, Madam Chairman, why would we spend $27,000 to find out what any business student could find out in a very short time, and probably knows anyway? Another firm, Hedlin Menzier and Associates, received a contract for $153,200 to provide assistance in the development of an initial exploratory forecast for transportation in Canada and to assist in a final report. Once again, this poor huckleberry from Hastings county has trouble understanding why we are spending $153,000 on this.
I see my time has just about run out, so perhaps we could have some idea from the minister why it is we spend hundreds of thousands-yes, millions of dollars hiring consultants when we obviously have a very talented staff at our disposal.

Madam Chairman, the hon. gentleman wants to know why some of the answers are not satisfactory. I suggest he has only to read the questions that he just asked a few minutes ago. I do not know how any intelligent man can intelligently answer such questions. He simply cites the figures without disclosing what is behind the figures, what is behind the research, whether it is important or not. Because we speak about concepts and conceptual frameworks or schemes, he finds it difficult. I do not find it very difficult; it is easy. Anyway, I will copy the questions he has asked and I will send them to all the people in my riding so they can see what kind of questions are put to the Minister of Transport.
You will probably get some answers, too.
I will double my majority.
On a question of privilege, what does the minister think I am going to do with some of the answers he has given me? I am going to send those to the people in my riding.

The first question had to do with the increase in overhead of 108 per cent, which is quite an amount. I must repeat what I have already said; if the hon. member had had a pencil at the time he would not have needed to ask the question. Some 45 per cent of this increase is for the Cornwall institute, and this is a 20 per cent increase in man-years. That adds up to 65 per cent. As for the rest, I will find out and give him the details, but it is something that can be easily answered. There is no scandal. It is the kind of increase we meet almost everywhere, in all institutions and in all departments, and even in private enterprise.
As for contracts that are awarded outside the government, a case can be made on that, too, but not in the way the hon. member made it. For example, should we have a permanent staff of engineers to build airports, or should
Business of Supply
this be done under contract by outside engineers? Should we have a group of architects that are civil servants, and should we tell them to design all buildings for the government, or should this work be done under contract by outside architects? We do have, of course, a corps of engineers and a corps of architects who exercise control and help us in our work, but the best way is to get some outside engineers on many occasions. Take an airport like Pickering or Mirabel; we do not build those every day.
That is not what the hon. member asked you.
He simply referred to contracts without defining anything.
He told you what the contracts were for.

As for professional and special services, these totalled $85 million for the department, $53 million for the government and $32 million for outside firms. I agree we can discuss the philosophy of this, but not the fact that specific contracts were awarded.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. minister, but his time has now expired.

Madam Chairman, I have a few questions I wish to put to the hon. minister.
First, I should like to ask him a question concerning an inquiry he ordered to study the causes of losses of lives and fishing vessels on the Pacific Coast. He ordered that inquiry recently, and I should like to ask him whether he has yet received the report and whether he intends to include in the legislation the recommendations contained in the report.

Madam Chairman, we have received the preliminary report, the report on the first inquiry on the above-mentioned causes; this report, as such, is not for publication for the obvious reason that several of the witnesses who appeared before our own investigators would refuse to do so if they knew that their names would be used publicly. Whether you like it or not, that is the way it is. Usually, in such circumstances a formal inquiry is held afterwards and is used as basic documentary evidence.
In this case, the preliminary report is complete enough to allow us to readily suppress names and to submit a substantial summary so that members of parliament are made aware of what happened. As soon as I can have the report translated into French, it will be tabled in the House.

I wish to thank the minister for his clarifications on that subject.
I should like to refer to another matter that relates to confused or combined jurisdictions as between the Department of Transport and the Department of the Environment. This occurred at a time when the minister's depart-
5700

May 12, 1975
Business of Supply
ment was responsible for certain shore rights and concluded an agreement with the developer of a marina at West Bay, near Esquimalt. I have had correspondence with the minister, and the confusion is being compounded. I have been assured by the minister that everything is in order and that the developer has fulfilled the terms of the contract and there have been no written complaints. I should first of all like to read into the record a portion of the terms of the contract completed between the department and the developer. It states:
That the lessee shall not... do, suffer or permit to be done, any act or thing in or upon the said land which shall or may be, or might become an annoyance, nuisance or disturbance to the occupiers of any lands or premises adjoining or in the vicinity of the said land-
There have been letters from people who are living in an area adjoining this West Bay marina which was developed when the Department of Transport had the responsibility. People living in areas overlooking this marina have written me and I have sent copies of each of those letters to the Ministry of Transport. To suggest in writing to me that there have been no written complaints is not right. There were no written complaints to the municipality, and that is the context in which the reply was made, but there have been written complaints and the minister has them on his file. If he does not, I will certainly provide them.
The municipality resisted these written complaints and suggested these people should write to their member of parliament or to the Ministry of Transport. I feel there has been an attempt at a run-around here, in two senses: firstly, there is the suggestion that the terms of this contract have been lived up to. That is not the case, and I do not think it is right or proper for the Minister of Transport to indicate to a member of parliament that the terms have in fact been fulfilled when they have not. Secondly, as a result of the transfer of responsibility from the Ministry to Transport to the Ministry of the Environment there has been an attempt to suggest it is no longer the business of the Minister of Transport but that it belongs to the Minister of the Environment. This is just not good enough. The government has signed the lease; the minister signed in the capacity of a minister of the Crown. He has bound the Crown and the other signatory to perform certain things. To suggest now that this lease is being fully fulfilled is something I will not accept. I am going to keep at this until I get a satisfactory answer. Is there any clarification the minister or his officials can give now in respect of this matter? If that is not the case, I have a number of other questions.

Mr. Chairman, I will have to refresh my memory on this matter. Let me remind the hon. member of two things. Marinas have never been under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport, but always under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works. We do have what we refer to as the small craft harbours act which was operating under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport but was transferred to the Department of the Environment. Perhaps this is what the hon. member is referring to. If he is referring to a marina, then we have never had jurisdiction. This jurisdiction was transferred to the Department of the Environment a year and a half or two years ago.

I would ask the hon. gentleman through you, Mr. Chairman, whether he thinks I am the one that should be responsible, even if I signed the agreement, when that jurisdiction was transferred? The hon. member refers to an agreement that I do not remember. I will have to refresh my memory. If I signed that agreement, then the responsibility now lies with the Minister of the Environment. I do not suggest the government has been liberated from its responsibilities, but if there are some objections, they belong to the Minister of the Environment and not to the Minister of Transport.

I thank the minister for that clarification and I point out that he signed the agreement in the name of Her Majesty, in right of the Minister of Transport, on April 26, 1973. The transfer of jurisdiction was subsequent to that but the binding aspect on the Crown is the same. What I object to is the issuance of erroneous information simply because the matter is now in the hands of another department. There are facilities for interdepartmental consultation.
There is another matter of interdepartmental relations to which I should like to refer. This is in relation to the loss of four tank cars filled with chlorine in the Strait of Malaspina. This happened about six weeks ago. The Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Transport have been saying different things about this. While I received some assurance the other day in committee, I should like to know whether the Minister of Transport will carry out the necessary salvage operations or make the facilities available to the company which claims to have found the cars containing this highly polluting material. Perhaps the minister would answer my questions.

I have just received this information, and have not been trying to withhold it. I am told that a search has been made and the chlorine rail cars have been found in deep water. I am informed that they intend to use a manned submersible in order to inspect the site to determine what can be done.

Again, I think these clarifications are worth having on the record. I am delighted we have got that far. We have to go a step further. We must get these chlorine tank cars out of the water. I understand there are facilities the Department of Transport can make available to a private contractor to undertake the salvage operation so that this pollutant will no longer be of danger to the community.
I should like to refer to earlier questions I raised in the House about safety measures for small craft, particularly commercial craft including tugs and fishing boats. Last October there was a question raised about the requirement of detector buoys or devices installed on tugs. I understand that regulations to that end were drawn up and ready for implementation, but there was some hesitation on the part of tugboat owners because of cost. I should just like to know where we are on this matter now because, for example, this would have saved a great deal of time in the search for the fishing vessels which were lost at sea. Has there been some device on which aircraft or other vessels could home? This might even have saved some lives. So far as I know, 14 lives were lost on that particular occasion in a very short time, a matter of ten days, and some 10 or 11
May 12, 1975

vessels. The installation of such safety devices on board commercial vessels before they put to sea would assist enormously in finding them in time to save lives and, of course, the vessels and their contents. Are we any further ahead with these regulations?

Madam Chairman, I will answer in greater detail after the dinner recess, if I have the opportunity. However, I remember very well-and now I am speaking from memory-that it was impossible to install these devices even in small tugs because the devices were too heavy. I do not say that we cannot find a device for smaller craft. Perhaps we can and perhaps we should, and this is what we are looking into now.
Do I still have some time left, Madam Chairman? May I ask a couple more questions?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Yes, the hon. member has some time left.

My next question relates to marine traffic control regulations. I believe there are some installations now being prepared or installed in Vancouver for remote monitoring of traffic coming in from the Pacific through the Strait of Juan de Fuca and up into the Straits of Georgia. There are LORAN or other similar types of radar installations along the coast so that incoming vessels may be followed. There are, presumably, shore to ship radio communications installed, and a general program for bringing in the ships in very much the same way as aircraft are brought in for night landings or through fog. In addition to the work being done by Canadian authorities, what consultations are there with Americans to combine their particular traffic operation with any operations on the Canadian side-a starboard-in starboard-out type of operation, for example?

speechtext: Order, please. The time allotted to the hon. member has now expired.

Madam Chairman, I want to take the opportunity today to discuss a couple of areas in transportation that are of real concern to me. Earlier I heard one hon. member opposite, I believe from the Stratford area, discussing rail passenger traffic in southwest Ontario. That subject does not have a great deal of direct effect on my constituents but it is something about which I have some personal knowledge, having grown up and moved through different places within southwestern Ontario, and having relatives living in the area of the Bruce peninsula.
I am sure the minister does not have to be reminded of the unanimous agreement of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications in the 1968 to 1972 parliament that railway passenger transport should be put back into full operation in the general southwestern Ontario grid complex. I should simply like to encourage the minister, if I can, to give this the highest priority possible when he is considering the over-all issue of developing a general rail policy in Canada. I am sure the benefits of such a program would be overwhelming for the people of southwestern Ontario, and of other parts of the country, where
Business of Supply
there is density of population and where railway systems are not being put to their full use. I have the same sympathy for the development of efficient rail passenger systems from isolated communities of some population to more densely populated communities.
When you consider the cost and efficiency of rail traffic as against the passenger car-the railway car handling 40 to 60 people versus 30 or 40 automobiles for the same number of people-when you consider the fuel factor, the cost of road construction and the use of viable farm land for such construction, one realizes-and I am sure the minister and his officials agree-that railways can play a vital role in the transportation policy that I spoke about in the last election campaign, and which I look forward to helping to develop as a member of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications in this parliament.
In talking about the development of a rail grid in an over-all transportation policy I would like to suggest that another priority is the triangle formed of Ottawa, Montreal, and Toronto. It is vital. Often I hear from my friends in the west and in the east, and those who talk to me from the north, that attention is always focused on southern Ontario, Montreal, and Toronto. When I speak about the importance of a highspeed, efficient, rail system between these three cities-our two largest and most active commercial centres, as well as the nation's capital-I am not talking only of the benefit to the people who live within that densely populated triangle but also of benefits for the people from other parts of Canada who must do business with the government or with their counterparts in these cities. To them as well that kind of rapid communication between these three centres is vital.
It is not only passenger service for people within that area but also tourist traffic that would benefit from rapid communication so that people will be able to travel to our capital which has been developed, at the cost of so much Canadian taxpayers' money, into perhaps the most beautiful capital in the modern world. The Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto grid is vital to any national rail transport policy.
The second point I want to make is one to which I hope the minister will give serious consideration. I should like to spend a moment or two addressing myself to the issue of airports, and specifically to the problem we had with airports in the Toronto area. I think I have been one of the most outspoken people in favour of the development of the Pickering airport. I know that the minister and the government have taken a considerable amount of heat in finally arriving at that decision. I also have had the personal experience of meeting women who have to stay around the house in daytime and who suffer nervous breakdowns as a result of the tremendous noise pollution in the vicinity of the Toronto international airport. Coming from a very large riding with a population Qf
150,000	I can talk about 30,000 to 40,000 people living with noise levels beyond tolerance, so when I stand in support of the development of Pickering I think I stand in defence of my constituents and their right to a decent lifestyle in a proper environment.
You certainly cannot tell people in public housing who live along those flight paths, or the several thousands senior citizens who live in large complexes directly in line with the runways, that it is their fault and that they

should have known ahead of time about the disadvantages of living there. Nor could you say to the people who live in moderately priced homes in the vicinity of the airport and have lived there for 15 to 20 years that they should have been able to predict what technology would bring in the development of air traffic in Canada.
I am pleased that the government has taken this difficult decision and I believe that in the long run, if the government of Ontario can say no to the Spadina Expressway to protect people in the downtown core, to improve their health, and if the city of Toronto can stop the development of high rise business complexes in downtown Toronto for the protection of the environment, then our federal government is acting similarly to protect people who are not immensely wealthy but who have the right to a decent environment.
Having said that, I noted in my mail in the last week or two considerable concern about the announcement of plans for passenger terminal expansion at Toronto international airport. An assurance was given in 1968 when the minister of transport at that time said that there would be no new runway expansion, and no new expansion of existing plans at Toronto international. But he also said that did not mean they would not go ahead with the plans as they were then on the books; these would have to be proceeded with because of a projected increase in traffic, and there would have to be adequate passenger facilities. I have explained that to my constituents who have written to me, and I support the minister. I know he is living up to the word of the government of that day when he announces that there will be some expansion of Terminal
2.
As I see the expansion which has now been announced; it will still not be as great as that which was on the bdoks in 1968 when the commitment was made. But having talked about people in my area having hope of relief some years down the road because of Pickering, and knowing that in Pickering, thank goodness, we will have learned from mistakes in planning and lack of foresight at all levels of government which could not foresee the development and rapid advance of air passenger traffic at Malton, I hope similar mistakes will not be made at Pickering.
Comparing the number of people who will be displaced at Pickering with the number of people in areas beyond noise tolerance in my area, the percentage at Pickering is minuscule indeed. Meanwhile the proper buffer zone can be put in and still leave far fewer people disrupted. And I suggest that in many cases people who live in that area come from other parts and have taken the opportunity to live in older homes and have advantages most Canadians do not have.
The argument about losing excellent farm land is nonsense, to my way of thinking. I know the area extremely well, and a great deal of that land is occupied by gentleman farmers or landed gentry, in the sense that they do not work the land. In some cases they do rent it to farmers, and more will be in use as farm land with the development of Pickering than at the present time.
It concerns me that in my area, with the expansion we have because of the new terminal facilities going in at

Toronto international, and because we know Pickering, even in its most minor development, will not be operational for several years, my people will not only not gain immediate relief from the very real noise problem they have, but the noise will grow worse until Pickering is started. When Pickering brings them relief, they will be lucky if it rolls back to the current intolerable level.
I wonder therefore, if the minister is giving consideration to ordering the installation of noise suppressors on Canadian aircraft. I realize it is difficult with international carriers, but Canadian aircraft carry the majority of passengers in Canada. I wonder whether the department is considering forgiveable loans, say forgiveable loans according to the sizes of the fleets of the airlines involved, and whether it would even consider, as a priority, trying to modify noise levels on the worst offenders, which are the DC-8's, if I am not wrong.
Mir. Alkenbrack: Madam Chairman, I have a couple of points I would like to inquire about.
Madam Chairman, on a point of order, have I used up all my time? If not, I wonder if the minister might respond to my questions.

Madam Chairman, I agree entirely that we should improve and exploit, much more than we have, the passenger train system. As far as the parliamentary committee is concerned, I hope that we will have the opportunity of discussing that, because there are many aspects. We have met several times with the government of Ontario to study which lines to develop. We have an agreement on the Richmond line, and we are about to reach an agreement on another line, which corresponds with the suggestions of the hon. member.
I agree entirely that we should use passenger trains much more than we have in the past. There is no doubt that there is a natural corridor where the bulk of the population in Canada resides, from Quebec city to Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto and Windsor. In this corridor I think there should be a very efficient passenger train service. I agree with the hon. member on that too. These are not the only places in Canada where trains are needed. Trains are needed in Vancouver, Hamilton, Calgary probably, Edmonton and Winnipeg. There are other places, but I think there should be good service where there is a concentration of population. This is something we will try to achieve.
With regard to the airport, I think that the hon. member is aware that if we are having so much trouble it is because we stuck to our word. The people of Malton were promised that Malton would not be expanded in terms of runways, but there is no doubt that we have to expand in terms of terminals. If runways ever have to be extended, they will be extended without increasing the noise level. It is not only the noise of an aircraft which is important, it is also the frequency of the noise. We have to take both elements into account. We must consider the number of planes landing and the noise produced by each aircraft. When Pickering is in operation there is no doubt that it will have an impact on Malton, unless by that time the number of flights has increased so much that the present situation at Malton recurs. We cannot of course foresee
May 12, 1975

exactly what type of aircraft will be in the air in 1977 or 1978, but this is something about which we will be careful.

Madam Chairman, I have two points I wish to bring to the attention of the minister at this time. The first is that of railway crossing protection. I have always been interested in railway crossing protection, and I am sure all hon. members and the minister have always recognized its importance. Since we are now in a period of depression and unemployment, why could the government not start a concerted program, and an increased and enlarged program to instal railway crossing protection devices? In my riding alone we had two allocated for installation recently on CNR crossings, and there are two more crossings urgently requiring protection, one at the Forest Mills CPR crossing in Lennox and Addington county, Richmond township, and another at Glen Tay on the same line of the CPR in Bathurst township, Lanark county. I remind the minister that it would seem to be a good idea for us to press for more railway crossing signal devices.
My second point is a very unpleasant thing to bring up, but it is in regard to public safety, and I think it should be made known to the House and to the minister. I spoke to the minister some time ago about the Ernestown wreck last December 20 on the main line of the CNR at about 8.25 p.m. in the evening, of that day, where a westbound passenger train, No. 45, and an eastbound manifest freight, No. 318, were in a head-on collision. That collision took a total of four lives; two enginemen and a passenger lost their lives at the scene, and a fourth person died about a month later.
The blood of one of the engineers was analysed as having an alcohol content of .08. This was revealed as the result of an autopsy. This is the level of impairment recognized in highway traffic cases. In this age of increased use of all kinds of transportation, those who use the systems take it for granted that the person driving is sober, whether he be in charge of a train, bus, boat or aircraft.

The recommendations of the coroner's jury inquiring into the accident at Napanee are very important and I want to put them on the record for the guidance of the minister. I know he will press for these recommendations to be put into effect. The addendum to the verdict of the coroner's jury stated in part:
Train 318 proceeded at a higher than recommended speed prior to the collision. The presence of alcoholic beverages found in the engine, and the presence of alcohol as determined by an autopsy, is a probable factor in the failure of Train 318 to stop at the designated signal.
This was no doubt the cause of the head-on collision. The jury made a number of recommendations, two of which I should like to put on the record. Recommendation No. 5 reads:
To initiate a study immediately to determine the effectiveness of the General Rules of the Uniform Code of Operating Rules, the adequacy of the requirements of the rules and employee adherence thereto.
Probably the most important recommendation was No. 6 which reads:
The railways should set up standard surveillance procedures to monitor the fitness of train employees reporting for duty.
Business of Supply
That is the point I wanted to make this afternoon.
Recommendation No. 9 reads:
All operating personnel should be given a more frequent medical examination which would include co-ordination tests.
That recommendation probably is not the result of the proof that alcohol had something to do with this accident. It is more or less a recommendation made in the interests of the general health of train crews.
I am sure the minister will appreciate the importance of recommendation No. 11 which reads:
The conductor should meet with his train crew prior to boarding the train.
The conductor has always been the boss of the train, and that is still the rule. If the conductor met his crew before the train left I am sure he could see to it that the rules were adhered to and these recommendations carried out and observed as to sobriety of the crew.
That is all I wanted to mention and I would respectfully ask the minister to take cognizance of these things and to consult with the CTC and the railways to make sure these recommendations are implemented.

Madam Chairman, there is no doubt that we will get the report of the CTC on this accident. I agree entirely with the hon. member's comments on the coroner's report, although I am not sure about the effectiveness of the suggested meeting before the train leaves. I should like to discuss that and see if it is practicable. If the problem were not alcohol it might be drugs or something else, and the question is how we can control that. I really do not know. In this case it is referred to as being a probable cause of the accident, and it might happen sometimes on aircraft, which is even more dangerous. I think we should take all precautions we humanly can, but some of them are really useless. The only way is to fire the man and never let him drive a train again.
When we have the impartial inquiry suggested some people will have the almost exclusive duty of looking into the causes of accidents and their prevention. I think we can improve the system. I agree with the hon. member, and cannot put too much emphasis on what he has said.

Madam Chairman, I should like to ask the minister some questions about Air Canada. We know it is a troubled airline and there is an inquiry going on at the moment. My questions are not related directly to the inquiry but to criticism of Air Canada long before the inquiry was initiated.
Certain questions have been raised by newspaper columnists and I should like to take them up with the minister now. When dealing with Air Canada in recent months has the cabinet committee refused to accept Air Canada's budget for future purchases of aircraft? If so, did Mr. Pratte, Chairman of Air Canada, refuse to give an explanation when asked about the purchases?

Madam Chairman, we have not refused, we have agreed. I know that Air Canada cancelled ten or twelve aircraft that were on order, but they did that themselves.
The hon. member says that Air Canada is a troubled airline, and I take exception to that because it is not true.

May 12, 1975
Business of Supply
Air Canada is a very good airline, one of the best. I believe that if the same kind of inquiry were made into other airlines we would find that Air Canada is better than most. We have not refused the budget of Air Canada because, if we had, it would not be flying today.
