speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock the hon. member for Dauphin had the floor.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a few more questions about Air Canada? It has been widely reported that Mr. Pratte and Mr. Baldwin have engaged in a series of running battles since 1968, or since assuming command positions. At the beginning, was not Mr. Pratte's function to plan policy and make long-range projections and was not Mr. Baldwin, as president, to run the airline? Am I correct in this? was this the general plan? I believe the appointment of Mr. Pratte was a new departure for Air Canada.

Mr. Chairman, so far as I remember the job of Mr. McGregor was split in two and we appointed a president and first vice president, or chairman of the board, I believe, exactly as we did with the CNR. The head of the railway company was Mr. MacMillan, whose job was split in two. Now Mr. Bandeen is president of operations of CNR and Mr. Taschereau is chairman of the board. Something similar was done with Air Canada.
Mr. Chairman, is the minister aware of any long-standing disagreement between those two top officials of Air Canada in the last five or six years?

Mr. Chairman, no, I am not aware of all the personal relationships in our Crown corporations, as I have six or seven under my jurisdiction. If I were to decide to inquire into the personal relationships of officers, it would take up all of my time.

It has been suggested that the appointment of Mr. Long has created difficulties in Air Canada, that he has been given little responsibility, and that all vice presidents have direct lines of communication to the chairman of the board. In other words, it is suggested that Mr. Pratte had assumed much greater authority than he should exercise, and that is one of the reasons why Air Canada has become involved in misadventures. Is the minister satisfied that the top management of Air Canada is satisfactory, and is he satisfied with the way Mr. Pratte has carried out his duties in Air Canada?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman knows that I cannot very well answer such a question. If he were to ask me if I am happy with the

structure of Air Canada, the CNR, the seaway authority, the CTC, the Northern Transportation Co. Ltd. or the National Harbours Board, I would tell him that, generally speaking, I am not satisfied with the way Crown corporations are structured. There should be more uniformity in their makeup. I do not say they should all be exactly alike, because they do not all fill exactly the same functions. At present they are constituted in such different ways that I do not know if they are to report to me, to parliament, or to the department. They were established to fill different needs. For example, Polymer Corporation is quite different from the others. I think the makeup of some was determined largely by how Mr. C. D. Howe felt when setting them up.
Shame!

I tell you Air Canada is a good airline. Is there friction between the officers of the company? I do not know, but I presume so, because all my life I have been involved with organizations and I do not know of any, including the one of which we are members, which is a model for all organizations, in which there is no friction at all.

Mr. Chairman, it has been charged that Air Canada management below the top level has been subjected to what are known as reorgs. Apparently reorg has followed reorg, if I may use the company's vernacular, and the morale of long service employees at the middle level has been damaged. Does the minister feel that this charge is correct, and is it true that Air Canada executives below the top level have been subjected to an abnormal amount of interference, which has contributed to fear among employees?

Mr. Chairman, I have no yardstick with which to answer such questions intelligently. I know that some people like Mr. Pratte; others think he is not good. Some people told me Mr. MacMillan is a great man; others that he is not so good. Some people told me that Mr. Sinclair is tops; others that he is a bully. I cannot make any judgment of that kind.
What do people say about the minister?

Mr. Pratte has suggested at various times that Air Canada does not compare favourably with other airlines because it flies too many short haul routes. Does the minister think the airline makes too many short haul flights, and does he plan longer hauls for the company's aircraft? Also, are tariffs to increase for short haul flights, in accordance with Mr. Pratte's suggestion?

Mr. Chairman, we could have a very long discussion about how the long haul and short haul should be balanced. Because Air Canada is a Crown corporation owned by the state, it must do things that other companies do not do. For example, last year Air Canada lost about $1 million on the Montreal-Moscow route. As a state we feel we should have a link with Russia which is a very important country.
Air Canada is asked to provide certain services that we cannot ask private enterprise to provide. Therefore when
May 12, 1975

you compare the financial statement of Air Canada with another company's which does not need to meet these obligations, that is unjust.
It is true that in the airline business long hauls are much more beneficial than short hauls. Some companies prefer only long hauls, leaving the short hauls to other companies. However, Air Canada has to fulfill both jobs because we need airline service between Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto, Calgary, Edmonton and Vancouver. That is its duty. Even though it means a deficit, it is for the welfare of Canada. It does not have anything to do with the quality of administration of the company.

If Air Canada does not find short hauls lucrative, why did it oppose the application by Nordair to fly from Montreal to Sudbury and Thunder Bay? In presenting its case Air Canada proposed fares considerably lower than Nordair which expected to have losses for three years before building up any traffic. If Air Canada does not find short hauls to its liking, why in this case did it not allow the private company to take the loss? Why did it oppose the application to the CTC?

Mr. Chairman, are we going to give the short hauls to the regional carriers, the long hauls to CP and get rid of Air Canada? That is not the way I look at it. I do not want us to be in the same situation as the United States where there are many regional airlines. If an airline that starts flying from Hamilton to Winnipeg and eventually to Regina is classed as a regional carrier, I think that is stretching the concept of region.
The problem is that the regions are not very well served. The reason is that the regional airlines want long hauls because they have jets, and with jets there is only one way to make money, that is, to have long hauls. If we are going to give the long hauls to the regional carriers, let us sell the other two airlines. Maybe we should have five national carriers in Canada. That is nonsense in this kind of country.

Mr. Chairman, Mr. Pratte has mentioned that he does not feel regional carriers should be involved in the charter business to any extent. He suggests that regional airlines with 707's or DC8's should give up this kind of equipment to Air Canada. Does the minister agree with Mr. Pratte that Air Canada should be the only airline with charters, and that the regionals should not be able to enter the charter business, particularly if they cannot use the 707's and DC8's which, I presume, are the large types of aircraft?

Unfortunately I have not read that statement by Mr. Pratte. Possibly I could see the text. Mr. Pratte never mentioned to me that that is an objective he is trying to attain. There is another airline in Canada, Wardair, which deals exclusively with charters. We may very well have charters during the busy seasons so that the main airlines do not need to have five, six or seven large aircraft that will be used only during a short period of the year. However, I do not think there should be five or six national airlines in Canada because most of them would be bankrupt within a few years.

Mr. Chairman, as the old saying goes: "If at first you don't succeed, try and try again." That applies, I believe, not only in literature but also in politics, since in order to reach one's objectives in politics, one must often try again. In the area that I represent, we have set ourselves the following objective: we are aiming to attempt to benefit fully from our geographical position and from our potential, to develop as fittingly as possible our part of the country.
I ask the House the following question: In the area of Windsor, in one area of Alberta or in any other area in Canada, would an unemployment rate of 30 per cent be easily accepted? Would it be accepted that municipalities, as there are some in my riding, where 90 per cent of the people live on social welfare, should have to demand positive and efficient actions from our government for the development of our country?
We have had in our area studies upon studies, more than anywhere else in Canada. The BAEQ cost $5,700,000 to the Canadian government; later on, we had various studies on transports, communications, regional economic expansion, representing expenditures of $10 million for an area of approximately 300,000 people. However, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), who was minister of Regional Economic Expansion, was the first to conclude that the studies were outdated, that at the very time conclusions were arrived at, the problems were of a different nature and that those conclusions did not really solve the problems that we faced.
We still face the same problems and the member who is now speaking to you is really aware of the problems of the under-developed areas. The people who were claiming the right to an harmonious development deserved more than statements and studies, but effective measures and a real leadership. In order to run for Parliament, I demanded that the Right Hon. L. B. Pearson promise, not only as future prime minister of this country but as leader of the Liberal Party of Canada, not to keep on with studies but to build a deep-sea harbour and provide for a year-round ferry service between both shores because I am one of those who, like Bossuet, believe that common sense is to be found in common people. It was believed that such was the essential tool for its proper development and that besides studies, there should be concrete projects to put an end to frustration and insure the people that the area in which they live has possibilities and that men in public life understand that.
I know that it is said in my party: Equality of opportunities to all Canadian people to benefit from the resources and advantages provided to us by this country and our political system of government. We believed that the development instrument we were asking for was essential to our development. Numerous studies had drawn the same conclusion. When we called for that project, it was not because we had ITT, Iron Ore or all kinds of big corporations backing us, but because we really wanted to benefit from our geographical advantages, from the fact that the St. Lawrence River has tremendous depths, as much as
1,000	feet, which would enable ships of the new generation to come to the inner part of this country, insure in our area a rational and normal development and revitalize all

May 12, 1975
Business of Supply
the St. Lawrence Seaway, the harbour of Quebec and those of Trois-Rivieres and Montreal.
And today the objections are basically the same as when at one time development of the St. Lawrence Seaway was sought; the port of Montreal objected to it because it was cut for a terminal function and it felt that with the extension of that seaway toward Thunder Bay it could lose that function. But after the St. Lawrence Seaway was opened, the port of Montreal saw its traffic increase fivefold so that if there were difficulties afterwards it is not because the seaway interfered with its development, but on the contrary it gave it a very large boom, and one should look for the problems elsewhere.
Today, there is a new phenomenon which is the new generation of ships. Are we going to turn that same seaway, as one slogan puts it, into a speedway for ships or are we going to continue as in the past to revitalize all along its shores industrial and commercial developments. Will we be stupid enough to give progress a cold shoulder, we who in the mining and energy areas, and in many other areas-perhaps that is not so accurate-but from the stand point of our resources and their development, are so dependent upon the United States that we will also be so for both the export and import of all our products. President Nixon himself stated that he would make sure they did not depend on Canada for their imports and exports; even if they did not have the natural seaports, they would build man-made ones in order to accomodate the new generation of ships.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think I could illustrate the feeling of frustration that exists in my area better than by reading textually a resolution of the city council of Riviere-du-Loup, adopted on Monday May 5, 1975, which reads as follows;
Whereas the Department of Transport of Canada has already stated that the Canadian government would do nothing more for the Gros-Cacouna port as long as a serious plan would not be issued with respect to its use;
Whereas the Havre-Champlain (Scott-Misener) company is ready to carry out in Gros-Cacouna a very important project for the loading and unloading of bulk dry cargo and has for many months submitted that project to the federal as well as provincial authorities;
Whereas, after reviewing the said project, the Minister of Transport of Canada said the federal government would make no decision in that respect as long as the port policy of the government of Quebec would not be known;
Whereas the aforementioned policy has been known for over two months and whereas the premier of Quebec said publicly at the beginning of April 1975 that the government of Quebec fully supported the development of the port of Gros-Cacouna and approved of the Havre-Champlain project, which the Quebec minister of Commerce himself did several months earlier;
Whereas, in spite of all the aforementioned, the minister of Transport of Canada is still hopelessly reluctant and, according to medias, wrote very recently to the premier of Quebec and told him that the federal government would not commit itself blindly into the development of the Gros-Cacouna port, and before anything was decided, the Canadian government and the government of Quebec would have to undertake joint preliminary studies ...
Studies again-
. .. into the cost of facilities and the feasibility of a mixed (government and private) ownership system for the Gros-Cacouna port facilities; Whereas all those hesitations ...
This is a polite way of putting it when you consider the frustration that exists in my area-

... seem to indicate that the federal government, rather than approving a job creating project, prefers to see 15 to 30 per cent of the people able to work collect unemploymant and welfare benefits;
Whereas the citizens of our area are fed up with studies of all kinds and know that several studies have already concluded in favour of the port of Gros-Cacouna (Brochu, Sores, Camus, Lalonde & Valois, C.D. Howe, etc. reports);
Be it therefore resolved,
Councillor Romeo Bossinotte moved
Seconded by councillor J.-Jean Dionne,
That this council: 1) urge most strongly the Minister of Transport and the government of Canada to approve immediately the Havre-Champlain project for the ferrying of bulk dry goods to the port of
Gros-Cacouna;
2) invite the Minister of Transport of Canada to come, in the last week in May or the first days of June, 1975, and meet with the municipal council and representatives of the Riviere-du-Loup Industrial Promotion Corporation, the Gros-Cacouna Port Promotion Committee and the local Chamber of Commerce, for a frank and constructive discussion about the port of Gros-Cacouna.
Mr. Chairman, my questions deal with those two resolutions: approval of the project and discussion with local authorities-

No, Mr. Chairman, this is not a speech but a point of order. We did agree that the hon. minister's time in replying would not be counted as time taken by the hon. member who was asking the questions, so I would like the Minister of Transport to give an answer to the quite relevant questions I asked him.

Mr. Chairman, as I have mentioned several times in the last few months, I understand that the members of the House are rather impatient, because they are anxious to see the result of our efforts not in the field of the reorganization of our Department, but of the reorientation of its economic and social philosophy.
The port system, Mr. Speaker, is one of the issues that were examined in depth. One of these studies was followed by the Scott report, because Mr. Scott was responsible for it. This report must still be dissected before it can be handed to me officially and then presented to the cabinet. I realize quite well that my hon. friend from Riviere-du-Loup is defending as always his constituents with a lot of enthusiasm and sincerity and I cannot blame him for that. However, I could not at this time state my views on the Gros-Cacouna project as long as there has been no final decision on a port development policy for Canada.
What is taking place in the area of ports is similar to what is taking place in other areas-and this is in line with a suggestion I have already made in the House-a number of ports come under the National Harbour Board,
May 12, 1975

others under port authorities or private administration, and still others under the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. We are trying to tidy up the whole port facility scheme, so that each port may serve its own purpose and refrain from destructive competitive action.
That is the problem we are faced with now and why Gros-Cacouna has yet to receive a reply. I take due note of the resolutions which have been adopted, even if I feel some of them should be redrafted, but I appreciate the reasons they were put together this way, in view of the very serious problems the area as a whole, but more specifically the Riviere-du-Loup, region is faced with.

Mr. Chairman, entering into this debate tonight on the Minister of Transport's estimates, I welcome the opportunity. The main question I should like to mention is freight rates in the interior of B.C., or the non-competitive freight rates, and whether or not they are fair; and exports into the United States and whether the transportation companies of Canada are holding their end up in this export field.
We in the interior of B.C. have been long suffering as far as freight rates are concerned, and I should like to take the few minutes at my disposal to explain some of the reasons. I have been involved in freight rates for the fruit industry of British Columbia for quite a few years but it seems we are not able to get our points of view across.
Since becoming a member of parliament I have had many representations from people in the industry in my riding, complaining and talking about freight rates and how they seem to be discriminated against. We are, of course, in a non-competitive area and it would appear that the transportation companies take whatever the traffic will bear. A couple of weeks ago when we were in Prince George hearing representations from many of the industries there, almost every organization that came before us had something to say about freight rates. It sounded exactly the same as what we had been going through in my riding for years in the fruit industry.
I had a phone call today from a businessman in my riding who did not know or realize that we were going to enter into this debate, but what he told me is similar to what has been going on for a number of years in the interior of B.C., where it would appear there is a non-competitive rate and that transportation companies take whatever the traffic will bear.
For instance, you can ship to Vancouver from eastern Canada and back to Prince George for less than you can ship through the CNR directly to Prince George. The marshalling yards in Vancouver become crowded and they have a lot of problems there resulting in the tie-up of freight. Nevertheless, with the type of competition there, you can go into Vancouver, and in fact from there into the interior, for less money than if you go directly into the interior itself.
I think the first time I was exposed to these freight rate anomalies was when I found that we could load apples in Kelowna, ship them to Winnipeg, unload them, put them in cold storage, a month or so later take them out of cold
Business of Supply
storage, load them up again, ship them to Florida, and get a rebate on the freight rates. That sort of thing was actually happening. What did we do in order to be able to get some competition? We would actually truck fruit across the border, load it on to American rail lines, send it to a border point just south of Winnipeg, unload it, put it on trucks and send it up to Winnipeg, and it would be cheaper to do so. We had to do this kind of thing to show up our situation. The businesses in B.C., most of them small businesses, were not able to do this.
The result was that we could get agreed charges. This was quite good. We could get these agreed charges until the last few years. The railways were not able to supply enough, or did not supply enough cars to hold up their end, and so the agreed charges had to go; they could not ship the percentages they agreed to ship, although they would have liked to charge for them.
In the last two or three years we have had a shortage of rolling stock to roll fruit from western Canada, British Columbia, to eastern Canada. What happens is that the market gets filled by our competitor to the south, the United States. There was never any shortage of fruit in eastern Canada, but it was not Canadian fruit, mainly because we could not get the rolling stock from the railways. Today they are negotiating with the railways for some piggyback trailers on an agreed basis.
I am sorry to say that when these people asked me last fall, "What are we going to do? Are we going to get any transportation policy? Is our government going to do something about transportation in Canada?", I had to say to them, "I am sorry but the Minister of Transport gets up in the House and says that transportation is in a mess. We have been asking questions and we have had days of debate, but I would tell you that you had better get out and do some negotiating of your own because you are not going to get much of a transportation policy as far as I can see. You have to move your fruit to market; you have a responsibility to get it there". So now they are making contracts. They are looking for contracts today, and the contracts are all in the transportation companies' favour. This is why I say that we in the interior of B.C. are having a problem with non-competitive rates. I should like to ask the minister whether he has looked into these non-competitive rates, and are they fair?
I should like to say a few things about exports to the United States of our fruit and lumber, as well as other products from British Columbia. Industries there are getting absolutely nowhere with the transportation companies in respect of exporting products to the United States. These exports are very important to Canada's balance of trade position, as I am sure the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce would confirm. Are the transportation companies holding up their end in respect of these exports, making sure that we are able to get our products to the United States? Has the Minister of Transport told these transportation companies in Canada that they have a responsibility in this regard, or are the railway and transportation companies just saying there is no way that they will have a part in this?

I can assure the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, that the fruit industry in British Columbia is getting absolutely no co-operation in the export of its products to the United States. Those are the two main questions I wanted to ask today, and I hope the Minister of Transport is doing something about these situations.

Mr. Chairman, in addition to problems in respect of rates there were problems last year in the movement of fruit from the Okanagan Valley. I have been requested many times by members of parliament from that region to find boxcars in order that fruit can be exported expeditiously to the United States. However, when the hon. member states flatly that these companies did not receive any help, I suggest that is not true. I succeeded in convincing the CNR to send a certain number of boxcars for the purpose of exporting fruit from the Okanagan. Perhaps the CN did not provide as many as the industry wished, but there was a certain number sent at the request of the government, or because of the pressure of the government.
There was also a shortage of cars for the movement of lumber, as the hon. member mentioned. At that time we talked about the creation of a company to keep rolling stock in reserve so that when there are peak production periods this company could provide the rolling stock necessary, and in this way avoid any possibility of losing our markets.
The hon. member suggests that we should not rely too much on new policies because they may take a long time coming into place, or they may very well never come. Those who are aware of the history of transportation in Canada will realize that if, and I underline the word if, in a few months we can really produce a new policy in the field of transportation, we will have achieved something that has never been achieved since Confederation.
I am reminded of one inquiry on the subject of pilotage. In that case it took Mr. Justice Bernier six years to produce his report. I think probably he is entitled to his pension.
So are you.

Well, not yet. The report of the MacPherson Commission, as well as reports in respect of other inquiries, took years to produce, and years before we had any new policies on transportation. Of course you can say that you do not believe a new policy will be produced until you see it. That is a normal attitude and probably the same one I would take if I were sitting in the hon. member's seat which seems, on the basis of comparison, at this moment to be better than mine.
This is one of the problems which exists and which we are trying to correct because Canada is an exporting country and it is very important for us that we have fast, accessible and cheap transportation in order to maintain our export position and protect our international markets. This is vital, but of course transportation alone cannot accomplish this. If our ports are paralyzed because the grain handlers decide not to load the grain, we have problems. We in Canada should not have the kind of problems we had two years ago, which was a good year for fruit and a good year for lumber. At that time it was

impossible to provide enough cars to move total production. This is one of the difficulties we are trying to solve. You may not believe that we will succeed. I have no evidence to produce in support of my belief that we will, other than my good faith that we will succeed.

Mr. Chairman, I must say that at first sight, I like the procedure now being tried out in the House. It allows members to set forth problems that are peculiar to each of our areas and to take stock of the problems of interest to their area. I shall mention in support of my statement the remarks made by the hon. member for Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata (Mr. Gendron) a few moments ago. I think that the manner in which he has stated the problem of concern to him and to the entire population proves that our present procedure makes for a truly open discussion. Every member in the House tonight and every member who will read Hansard tomorrow may appreciate the seriousness of our proceedings.
Mr. Chairman, I know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) is responsible for a large department since it deals with surface, water and air transportation. The minister is no more amphibious than the member now speaking. The minister must be constantly aware of transportation problems and it is not always easy to solve them in a few words. It is obvious that he needs numerous officials. Besides, we have proof of this tonight in the House. There are some on the floor of the House and there are probably two dozens in the galleries who are following the debate. The minister is not in a position to know them all; it would be asking too much from him. However, they must trust him.
It happens that in his department like in others, some bureaucrats take themselves too seriously and think that the Department of Transport is their own business. They forget that members of Parliament are answerable to the people.
Having said this, I should like to take advantage of the consideration of the Transport estimates to deal with a problem which is not new, namely the dredging of the channel the water from the St. Lawrence to the Montmag-ny wharf. Last year-and the minister will surely remember, when the Department of Transport estimates were under consideration, I made representations in that connection and the minister had seemed willing then to settle this problem. I hope he is still favorably inclined. That dredging matter, although often brought up in this House by the members who preceded me here as representatives of my riding, has never been solved even if it has repeatedly been discussed; but I have every reason, I say this quite sincerely, that we are nearing a settlement, judging from the dialogues and exchanges of views we had in committees, or on occasion when I met various ministers. Still, and I say this without wanting to offend anyone, everyone holds to his opinions, according to the studies I have made; it has even happened, when the file was sent to the Department of Transports for a quick perusal, that the officials mainly stressed disadvantages of the situation, its non profitability, with the various responsible ministers. And then, it was required to show what benefits might result from the dredging of that channel for the development of some natural resources in that area.
May 12, 1975

I think that the various departments in the federal government were ready to cooperate, it would be possible to solve this problem and ensure that the development of the area between Quebec and the Gaspe peninsula, I mean the south shore of wich the city of Montmagny can properly be considered as the capital, since it is located in the centre of that area!
Until now, Mr. Chairman, in every development project that has been implemented under the various federal policies or with the cooperation of the province of Quebec, the south shore has always been overlooked. In the studies conducted, the experts have always considered Quebec City and the surrounding area. Then, they flew over the south shore in order to go and study the needs of the Gaspe area, as I know that there are also needs to meet there.
However, the south shore is not included in the area surrounding Quebec City, being located many miles away, nor is it close to the Gaspe peninsula, as it is even farther; it is a different area and I ask that it be considered as such and that special projects be designed for that area in order to ensure its development. I think that it will never be able to develop further if action is not taken to fully develop all its resources. There is no need to mention them all, they are numerous. That area has a tremendous potential for touristic development; the many islands located in the St. Lawrence river are part of the area and better communications are needed to reach them and make the most of them.
I also wish to remind you that Montmagny and the vicinity is a paradise for migratory birds, and particularly the snow goose. It will be recalled that the mayor of Montmagny, Dr. Gauthier, and all his council, in cooperation with the Chamber of Commerce and every organization in the area, started in Montmagny an annual Snow Goose Festival. I wish everyone could see at this season, from approximately 300 feet behind my residence, thousands of snow geese currently migrating to their summer nesting grounds, from which they will be returning next fall. This is an industry that should be expanded. But in order to do that, outsiders coming into the area should have access to the islands, in the fall, to hunt snow geese. This is a tremendous sport. Unfortunately, transport facilities are inadequate.
Since the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) is inclined to approve the renovation of the Montmagny wharf, I should like this evening to ask the Minister of Transport whether it is possible to very seriously consider whether, in turn, the Montmagny channel could not be dredged, so that the hunting and tourist industry may be further developed, and whether also a marina could not be built. I know this is not his responsibility, but somebody must take the lead to make things possible. Sheltered waters are needed so that small craft can take refuge during storms. This would be a suitable location if it was developed.
Second, I would ask the same thing I requested last year, and I am convinced I will have an answer since this item is again included in the estimates. I noted last year in the estimates a quite significant amount for the improve-
Business of Supply
ment of the channel opposite Cap-aux-Oies. I do not know if the minister remembers that.
In any event, there was amazement that $2 million were allotted for the improvement of the channel there. If I am misinformed, I hope I shall be corrected, but I am convinced this will be done this summer. I had an opportunity to discuss with pilots. I was told that the river is approximately 35 feet deep at that place. I wonder why this year a $925 million amount is again included in the estimates for 1975-1976. The sum of $925 million has also been forecasted for future years. If this is necessary, I do not object. It is very obvious that the channel must be maintained. Since the votes are here, if the Minister could use his authority to transfer these votes, which will be used to improve the channel, which would then be deep enough to allow normal navigation, maybe the channel from the river to the dock at Montmagny could be dredged.
Those are the few considerations that I wanted to bring to the attention of the Minister, very seriously and with a lot of heart, because I know that he is very concerned about the development of the area to which I have referred, like all the other areas of the country, and it is on behalf of all the organizations, which you will excuse me for not naming, that I am making this request; I am the spokesman for all the organizations which have already been named, and of which about thirty at least have been asking the same thing for many years. I hope that everyone is not wrong at the same time. I know in advance that the Minister will tell me: "Yes, this will take money". I understand this and so does everyone else, but if we wait for some garantee about the profitability of the service before doing anything, I think that we shall never do anything because there are public services now in operation which were supposed to be profitable and each year, the Minister has to come to Parliament and ask for new credits to set them afloat, to pay their deficits. It would not be any worse in Montmagny. I know that it would not be any better, but it would not be any worse.
I sincerely ask if it is possible to do something. I think that the government of the Province of Quebec would be willing to co-operate, as well as the Minister of Public Works and also the authorities of the city of Montmagny.
It is through co-operation that we will succeed in solving that issue and in providing the South Shore area with proper public utilities so that the standard of living and the per capita income of the South Shore population, which are unfortunately the lowest in Canada, may be improved. I would now ask the hon. minister to make comments on that subject.

Mr. Chairman, it was a real pleasure for me to hear again my good friend, the hon. member for Bellechasse who is asking again that there be dredging operations around the Montmagny wharf in order to allow better circulation between that town and the islands which are an extension to the Orleans Island.
The hon. member is right when he talks about the snow geese. It is a remarkable spectacle. It is not necessary to go there hunting, seeing them only is worth the trip. I believe that in such circumstances maybe he should make

representations not only to the Ministry of Transport which has a marginal responsibility, but also to the Department of Tourism, in Quebec City, and to the Department of Public Works. The latter is concerned with the maintenance of wharves and small harbours.
He could also contact the Department of the Environment which is in charge of harbours for small boats. It is a complicated issue but surely he could do something about it and, in my opinion, I think that by making representations to those departments, he will succeed in getting the water level around the Montmagny wharf raised in order to allow the boats to come there and to visit one of the most attractive towns in the Province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, to get his figures straight when he reads the budget, he should read $925,000 instead of $925 million; it is not quite the same thing. The total amount is $2,100,000: we did some dredging at Cap-aux-Oies, but there has been some filling up and efforts must be made to bring the depth of the channel down to 40 and 45 feet at high tide. If the hon. member can transform the $925,000 into $925 million, I promise we will do some dredging at the Montmagny wharf.
In any event, he will certainly get a sympathetic ear; but this is not something I can assure him of as a project we will achieve solely with assistance from the Department of Transport.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order.
I apologize to the hon. minister if I said $925 million. That was certainly a mistake because I did read $925,000. I would not want the House to get the impression that I intended to falsify the figures in the budget. My apologies, and I thank the minister for having pointed it out to me.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to use my 15 minutes, or part thereof, largely in asking the minister some questions about my part of the country. I was delighted, as were a number of my constituents, about the announcement by the federal government that it would be building a railway link between Ashcroft, Cache Creek and Clinton. This will be a link between the CNR and the CPR to the B.C. rail.
Many of my colleagues from the prairies, and on both sides of the House, realise that the Fraser canyon can be a very difficult bottleneck with respect to the two rail lines, especially during the winter time and spring break-up. There are often slides which can hold up trains going down the Fraser canyon for long periods of time. This link has much potential for the economy of this country and for the economy of that part of my constituency, and I would like the minister to inform the House of some target dates. I would like to know what schedule he is following now, what kind of work might be taking place at this time, and the target completion date. That is mostly what we are concerned about. We would like to have some idea of the framework in which the Government of Canada will be moving.
Another question concerning the people of Kamloops relates to terminal facilities. Kamloops is one of the most rapidly growing cities in the province of British Columbia,

and the number of passengers moving through the Kamloops airport in the past few years has probably been the most rapidly growing in the country, so the terminal facilities have really become quite inadequate over the past couple of years in particular. There have been some additions made to the facilities, which have been quite helpful both for onloading and offloading, but these are only temporary additions.
I have had a number of discussions with the minister's regional officials who have been very helpful, and I know they have a number of good plans on the drawing boards for terminal facilities in Kamloops. One date we had been kicking around, with regard to having the new facilities built, was 1977. I would like the minister to give me some indication of these possible new facilities in Kamloops and to advise whether that 1977 target date can be met or is realistic. Perhaps this was just in the very preliminary planning stages in his department, but I want to stress that it is very necessary that we have new and adequate terminal facilities in Kamloops as soon as possible.
The other area I was talking about with the minister's regional officials, and upon which I received co-operation, was the terminal facilities at Quesnel. They also had a number of good plans on the drawing boards for Quesnel. They just obtained jet flight service in there, Pacific Western Airlines, not too long ago. It is a service which has been very much needed, and it is warmly received by the people of Quesnel and that part of the Cariboo. I would like also to know what time schedule the minister and his department have for new terminal facilities in Quesnel.

Mr. Chairman, the negotiations between the federal government, the B.C. government, BCR, which is owned by the B.C. government, and the CNR have been long and complicated. I know there is an understanding and it is supposed to go on. I am not even sure that the formal agreement has been signed yet. If the hon. member wants the target as far as the Clinton-Ashcroft bypass is concerned, it is not supposed to go beyond 1978, so the target of 1977 is about right. This is something which is urgent and essential to the development of the region and for the normal circulation of goods in the direction of the B.C. coast and ports.
Unfortunately I did not catch the second question. Would the hon. member mind repeating it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
The second question related to the new terminal facilities in Kamloops. I mentioned that I had a number of productive conversations with the minister's regional officers who had been very co-operative. There are some good plans on the drawing board for new facilities. In casual conversations the officials told me to look at 1977 for the new facilities there, but this was not their decision and it had to go to Ottawa for confirmation. The facilities were improved recently for loading and offloading, but still they are only temporary facilities. We need permanent facilities in Kamloops, and in Quesnel as well, and I believe the plans are also on the drawing board.
May 12, 1975
If the hon. member does not mind I will take that question as notice and let him know tomorrow exactly what is the target.

Mr. Chairman, in opening I should like to say to the minister that I fully sympathize with him for all the reports with which he has to deal. There have been a multitude of them in the period since confederation. Unfortunately they have not been followed by policies. The reports have emphasized the problems which exist nationally and regionally, and it is now imperative to have policies.
There are some questions I should like to put to the minister. First of all, what is the depth of investigation by the minister or his staff into the branch line abandonment proposal of the railroads in respect of communities which may become isolated and put out of business if a branch line is abandoned? Secondly, what is the information on the revenue which will accrue to the main lines if the wholesale abandonment of branch lines becomes the policy of the two national railroad companies? Have these two questions been given proper appraisal?
Is the hon. member talking about branch lines generally?
That is right-not any specific one but just the basic policy on branch line abandonment, its effect on the community abandoned, and eventually on the traffic on the main line.

There is a definite policy as far as the branch lines in the western part of Canada are concerned where 12,000 miles are frozen till the year 2000, and 6,000 miles are going to be reviewed by a commission so that we will know exactly what we are going to do with them. They are not going to be abandoned before the end of 1975, however, and what happens after that will depend on the report. There are about 500 miles which everybody agreed should be abandoned for all practical purposes.

Madam Chairman, I do not think the minister intended to evade my question. He has given me the position at the moment on branch line abandonment as far as policy is concerned. I should like to know if there is an in-depth study on two aspects of the consequences of abandonment-first, the consequence to the community located on a line to be abandoned and, second, the consequences on total traffic on main lines which have depended on the branch lines as sources of traffic or feeder lines for the main lines. Is this under study? I have never seen it mentioned in any report relating to transportation.

Madam Chairman, I am not sure that I understand the question clearly. No branch line can be abandoned in Canada without approval by the CTC. This is not a policy but is the procedure to be followed in the abandonment of an active branch line. As far as the policy of the government is concerned, this has been talked about at the WEOC Conference. I do not want to evade the hon. member's question, but was he referring to the section of 12,000 miles, 6,000 miles, or 500 miles?

There are areas of Canada which have been served by one line or the other and part of the
Business of Supply
industrial background of those communities is still dependent upon the railroad and will be damaged if the lines are abandoned. I should like to know what happens to the main line if producers of traffic on the branch lines go out of business?

Madam Chairman, I reserve the right to correct myself tomorrow if I am mistaken, but the information I have at the moment is that the mandate of the inquiry is not limited to the western provinces. It is to make a study of all Canada and see what the economic impact will be if some branch lines are abandoned, whether in the maritime provinces, Quebec, Ontario or the western provinces. If my information is not correct, I will rectify it tomorrow.

I should like to point out that the area of the Saint John River valley, the Annapolis valley and other areas in Nova Scotia have been served by railroads. Instead of bringing forward applications for branch line abandonment, why do not railroads, all of them, make it their policy to seek out business? Without business they will be forced to abandon lines. I suggest that the policy of the government should put the onus on railways to search for business in areas in which they intend to abandon lines. Other enterprises, whether they are banks, chemical companies, fertilizer companies or beer companies, pursue business. This approach seems to be totally lacking on the part of our railway system.
Why should businesses-I do not expect the minister to answer but I wish the department would consider this- which are not familiar with the workings of the transport industry need to buy their own truck units in order to deliver their own products to their own customers, especially as many of these businesses have been served by the railways? This does not involve rates; this involves service. Service which was available to some of these businesses 10 or 15 years ago is no longer available, although the railway lines still run past their front doors. It seems to me that in seeking a solution to the difficulties of railways the minister should ask why so many companies have bought their own trucks?
Why does the Viau Company have its own trucks on the road? Why do Humpty Dumpty and Home Hardware have their own trucks on the road? Are these companies making money from trucking, or from manufacturing and merchandising? Further, are these companies, by entering the transport business, able better to serve themselves and at less cost than would be the case if we had a better rail transport system? Why should the publicly-owned CNR let this business slip out of its hands while other people, less experienced in the transport business, deliver products they manufacture, not because they want to, but because they must?
If the study previously mentioned is to be concerned about the east as well as the west, will guidelines be laid down regarding the consideration of the Maritimes or Atlantic area? Does the minister have any idea as to how profitable the CNR or CPR find Maritime region business? Also does the minister know, from cost submissions, whether the railways are making more or less profit than

May 12, 1975
Business of Supply
they ought to make, and what assurance can the minister give that the level of service in future will not fall below the level presently being supplied? What is the policy for improving service to Kelowna, Selkirk, Prince George and various other areas of the country? Can the minister comment on this question? After all, our economy cannot function adequately in the absence of a transportation policy. Such a policy is needed to help the economy.

Madam Chairman, perhaps my answer of a few minutes ago was wrong. If the jurisdiction of the commission is to be limited to western Canada, under our transport legislation a similar duty devolves on the CTC. This means that CN should apply to the CTC, and the CTC has to conduct an inquiry in order to justify any decision it might take. I will inquire and find out exactly the mandate of the special commission that was set up by the federal government.
The hon. member asked if the railways are making money in the Maritimes. I know that we are subsidizing the Maritimes.
And the west.

Yes, and the west. But the railways are not making money. This year they are all losing money. I would be surprised to learn they are making money in the Maritimes, but I will check and give the hon. member that information tomorrow. At the same time I will look into the other matters the hon. member put to me.

Madam Chairman, will the minister also ask the department to examine why so many people are going into their own trucking business, because once many of these companies were served by the railroads? How can they afford to do their own trucking, and why cannot the railways, the CNR, the CPR and other railways, do it more cheaply, especially when the rail lines already run past the front doors of these firms?
It has been recognized that an adequate transport system for the prairie areas and the west generally, primarily a rail transport system, is imperative if the agricultural industry of the region is to survive. An adequate rail transport system is equally necessary for the survival of agriculture in Kelowna, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and elsewhere. Such areas are equally in need of an adequate rail transport system. What policies will the minister advocate in order to allow the agricultural industry in this country to continue prospering? Further, what policies will the minister bring forward in co-operation with the Minister of Agriculture and his own departmental officials to make sure that the railways serve adequately the agricultural industry of the Atlantic area, at rates which will permit agriculture to make a profit?

Madam Chairman, the policy on which we are working, which has not been completed, concerns agriculture and all other sectors. We are convinced in the department that we must have a good railway service in this country. We need that in Canada. This country is too big to rely on trucking or other modes. We need a good railway system, not only for industry but for agriculture, too.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member who is about to rise, but his time has expired.

Madam Chairman, may I ask the minister a question concerning regional air carrier policy. I wonder if Air Canada service is to be substituted for regional carrier service in certain areas. I know the minister was interested in the Nordair application for the Ottawa-Sudbury-Thunder Bay route. Is there to be any substitution of service? I assure the minister that the flight, given present departure times, will not make money for Air Canada or anybody else. Perhaps someone could make money if the flight were at a different time. Does the minister intend to develop a new policy in this whole area, and how will we hear about it?

Madam Chairman, the last time we made an effort to elaborate an air policy in Canada was in 1966, I believe. Of course since then conditions have changed. I do not blame those who brought in the earlier policy. They did their best. Of course no regional carriers then operated jets. The business of regional carriers was to serve certain regions. Then they bought jet aircraft, DC-8s, DC-9s, Boeing 707s and 747s, and they put pressure on the CTC for new routes. They asked that Air Canada routes be given to them because they could not make money with jet aircraft on the kinds of routes they flew. Without doubt there is no money to be made in flying a jet from Brandon to Winnipeg.
But there is from Brandon to Toronto.

They can make money by flying from Brandon to Toronto, but not by flying from Brandon to Winnipeg.
We first tried to solve the problem of international routes. We announced last year how we are dividing the world and what kind of policy we are going to follow. However, we have not yet reached the regional carriers. At this time the policy is not designed. However, we intend to have one as soon as we have taken care of other urgent problems.

Madam Chairman, we have several problems with Air Canada. One is that it did not get all the international routes. We have two major air carriers in Canada, Air Canada and CP Air, which was probably a very bad mistake. Even France, Britain, and other countries considerably larger and more prestigious than Canada cannot afford that.
The minister stated that the regional air carriers have bought jets. That is true. They have bought them because Air Canada failed to meet the needs of travelling Canadians, particularly in the Caribbean. There is still a shortage in the Caribbean even with Wardair, Nordair, QuebecAir and Eastern Provincial.
I am sure the minister will agree that cutting out the regional carriers is not the answer. Nordair flies 727's and 737's into the Arctic. Air Canada should be doing that, but is not for two very good reasons. It does not have the planes that will fly in that area. Air Canada has bought
May 12, 1975

the wrong kind of aircraft. It is looking for prestigious international service which the Canadian people cannot afford. We are not in that field.
I have no objection if the minister wants to be a real nationalist about this. I would be quite happy if tomorrow he put in a system that would meet the needs of the Canadian public for air service with one airline called Air Canada. It has all the machinery. There is no doubt about it. It has enough vice-presidents to fly the damn things, if only they were capable of flying. However, they will have to provide the kind of aircraft that regional carriers are supplying.
I am pleased that after the problem of international routes has been solved, the minister is going to look into the regional problem. I suggest that when he does that, he look at another airplane for Air Canada. He should be buying the Dash 7. I understand that is a large Otter. Air Canada should be buying 30 or 40 passenger planes.
If we are going to run a Canadian airline, it should use jets. We should be using jets to fly these routes.
Has the minister given any consideration to security costs at airports? We are not catching anybody. I have heard that one or two members of parliament carried guns through security in one or two major cities just to try it. The system did not work out. I can explain, to anyone who wants to know, how to beat it. It is very easy to do.
I have to spend a lot of time in North Bay where I make my air travel connections. There are ten RCMP officers there. They receive at least $10,000 a year. That comes to $100,000 a year. Air Canada hires Pinkerton people. There are three main flights a day. I do not know how that kind of expenditure can be justified. One RCMP officer would be enough. The only purpose for their being there is to back up the Pinkerton people.
North Bay is a bad place.

The same is true in Sudbury, Timmins, Calgary and Edmonton. I never went through a search like that before. They made everyone almost strip because there was a girl who was going through with gilt buttons on her coat. If the machine will pick up the gilt, it will pick up anything.
What are we doing? Are we training people for the Olympics? Is this why we are training the RCMP? I do not see why we need ten RCMP officers, not in the whole North Bay area, but just at the airport. I rode on a Cessna 402. No one is going to take that very far. I often wonder if it will make it to Ottawa. The Otters will not go very far. They are the planes which go through North Bay most. Air Canada has two main flights a day with a DC-9. Has the minister given any consideration to the cost of security? This seems to be away out of line. We are not getting anything for our money.
One of the RCMP officers said he did not like his job. He said it would be fine if they would move him somewhere else where there is something to do because he does not like sitting around all day drinking the bad coffee they have in the terminal. North Bay, as the minister is aware, has been changed to eastern air defence. In case of bad weather, Earlton becomes the emergency auxiliary field. Has the minister given any consideration to updating the
Business of Supply
buildings at Earlton? There are 24 hour weather and radio personnel there, as well as a terminal. All the buildings those three agencies use are pre-war. They were built about 1935 or 1936. Even if it is just to save on heating costs, a small terminal could be built at a fairly reasonable cost. Has the minister given any consideration to this?
Madam Chairman, I do not know if I heard the hon. member correctly. He said that Air Canada should go jet all the way. At the same time he said it should buy Dash 7's which are not jet, but turbo.
They are not flying.

They are still being tested, but they are flying. Apparently they are good planes. Anyway, we will wait and see.
In 1965 or 1966, it was in the policy I referred to a few minutes ago, Air Canada agreed to give certain lines to the regional carriers. That is why lanes were given to Quebec Air, UAWA in British Columbia and TransAir in Winnipeg. They were not given to Nordair, but all the others. It was the policy of the government at that time, rightly or wrongly, and I have my opinion on this, to take away from Air Canada a certain number of lines in order to allow the regional carriers to make a profit. After that, they succeeded in stretching their routes and that is when they started buying the jets. When you buy a DC-9, even if it is a short conventional one, you need to have room. Otherwise you cannot economically operate such an aircraft. At this time Quebec Air has two DC-8's which it purchased recently for a charter to Europe. TransAir has a 747.
It is Wardair.

The hon. member is correct, it is not TransAir, but Wardair that has the 747.
In the United States they believed for a century that it was good to have as many railways as they could build, as many airlines as they could create. What happened? Half of them went bankrupt. Now even Pan-American Airlines is in trouble but has been saved by the banks. I would not like to see, one day, in our lap or in the lap of the opposition, one or two airlines which could not make a profit asking for a subsidy or new routes in order to keep going. I do not mind if we have to intervene more directly, but I believe it is preferable for the Canadian people to have healthy airlines which know what are their limits. Right now they do not know so they take chances, and one day the taxpayers are going to be called upon to pay the bill.
What about the cost of security and the minister's ideas as to its value?

We do not seem to have any problem at the moment. We do, of course, collect knives and articles of that kind from luggage. I do not think Canada is the most dangerous spot. The United States may be. After all, it is easy to come from the United States to Canada, and we do not want Canada to become a haven for hijackers. This leaves us with the necessity of putting some kind of security measures into place. I can tell hon.

May 12, 1975
Business of Supply
members that I am one who is probably the most allergic to these searches. Each time I come through, they do not even recognize me and I am screened like the others. When the hon. member talks about ten members of the RCMP in Thunder Bay or Sudbury-
North Bay.

They were there
accidentally.
Oh, oh!

Or because the hon. member was there! I know that in Montreal, though it is not as big as that city, I never see more than two at the same time, and I go there every week. In Toronto I have never seen more than two or three. Some are teaching, and some are backing up those who are making the search.

Madam Chairman, I have a series of questions which may not seem important to the minister but which loom rather large in my constituency, which depends so heavily on communications facilities. At the outset though, may I say I fully endorse the security measures being taken at airports throughout our country. If I had any complaint to make it would be against the stupidity of members of parliament, of all people, trying to test the system. All that has done is bring the security personnel down around our necks. I find myself now being recognized and singled out for a more thorough search than ever before simply because of the stupidity of some hon. members.
I should like to ask the minister to give me a status report on the terminal building at Whitehorse, which has been on the book for so many years but which has still not got off the ground. I want to ask the minister why his department is phasing out the radio ranges in the remoter areas where, in my view, they are still vitally needed. The latest announcement concerns the elimination of radio ranges in Whitehorse and Tasland and the replacement of those ranges by non-directional beacons. The beacons are fine for getting from one point to another but they help very little in getting down through cloud to a safe landing.
Would the minister inform me as to the status of the installation of emergency locater transmitters in aircraft registered for use above the 60th parallel? I believe the time has passed when the law requires installation of ELTs in all aircraft operating in sparsely settled areas. Has this been accomplished?
I want the minister to give me a report with respect to a matter which was mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, that is, the setting up of an independent body for the purpose of investigating aircraft accidents. This has been promised, and it is long overdue. I know the minister is in favour of it. It simply does not look right, for example, in the case of the last fatal aircraft accident in the north in which Panarctic was involved, that one of the major shareholders of the company, the government, should be the accident investigating body.
I want to ask the hon. gentleman when new and improved navigational aids will be provided at the airfield at Faro where traffic demands an IFR facility. I wish to complain vigorously about the placing of electric power

lines across the Yukon River at Whitehorse across the only available stretch of water which can be used for emergency landings by aircraft which have developed trouble on take-off from Schwatka Lake. These wires prevent safe take-offs and landings on that admirable stretch of river which is so essential to safe operating out of the lake terminal at Whitehorse.
I want to ask him, too, to exert whatever influence he may have with his colleague the Minister of Finance to get rid of that 10 per cent tax which has been placed on all new aircraft being imported into Canada for private owners, under the guise of some sort of fuel conservation plan. I believe there is not a member here familiar with general aviation who would object to the removal of this tax. Putting it in a more positive way, I believe every member, in all parties, with any knowledge of the general aviation industry, opposes the continuation of this tax. The minister should exert whatever influence he can to get it removed, because to an area such as ours where aircraft are so vital for getting around the country, it means a good deal to us to have 10 per cent added on to the cost of an aircraft.
I want to register my complaint, in what I hope will be taken as a non-bigoted fashion, in regard to the debate now going on with respect to the use of French and English in aircraft communications, air-to-air and air-to-ground. I think this can only have one result, namely, the impairment of safety standards in air transport. There is an international language of the air, and this country has been a signatory to it through ICAO for years now, and that language is English. If it were French, then it would be French; but it so happens that before the real debate on bilingualism developed in this country English was made the international language for air transport, and it should remain that way.
There are two accidents that can be directly attributable to the confusion caused recently over which language to use in the minister's own province. It is ludicrous to think that we may have French as well as English in air transport in Canada. This would mean rewriting, for instance, the international phonetic alphabet, which is now a combination of Latin and English words, which to me is silly.
If this were carried the whole way, we might find Air Canada and other international airline pilots doing cockpit checks in both official languages, which I think would be silly indeed. We should stick to safety standards and forget about the bilingualism debate so far as air transport is concerned.
I would also ask the minister to bring me up to date with respect to the rail studies in which the CNR is involved, so far as transportation in the Yukon territory is concerned. Studies have been undertaken in conjunction with other carriers and I should like to know whether those studies are ready to be reported; if not, when they will be reported; and what the feasibility is of interior rail into the Yukon connecting with the south.
Finally I want to register a complaint about telecommunications, something which falls within this minister's jurisdiction. His colleague, one of the "Three Musketeers", the Minister of Communications, came up to the Yukon on
May 12, 1975

a business visit a short while ago and, I will not say as a result of the visit, but coincidentally after he left, telephone rates went up. Telephone services in certain areas were discontinued, and other operators got bills that they had never received before for their telephone services.
The minister does not know about this. I was hoping he would be here, as he was this afternoon, so he would be made aware of it. I have written to him, but I dare say my letters never get to his level in the ministry.
There are emergency telephone services operated by CN Telecommunications which are now being cut out. These telephone services provide a very essential service. One might run across a highway in the Yukon where there has been an accident and there is no way of communicating and getting medical or other aid. These telephone services should remain for emergencies, if nothing else.
I want here to register a personal objection. Because all parts of the north are not blessed with dial telephones or the push button type, in the remoter areas we have to use radio telephone service. One of the most common in use is the single sideband SBX-11. A unit like this would require an initial investment of about $1,000, which the owner has to shell out in order to provide himself with communications. In my own case I have one in one of the remoter areas of the Yukon, and I use this unit for passing on weather information to the minister's department and for passing on information regarding lost aircraft, both to his department and to the RCMP-all for nothing as far as I am concerned.
I have now been told that in order to carry my identifier on the books of his department-that, in radio communications terms, is the telephone number, which in my case is Sierra Queen 950-I have to pay $7 a month. I think that is carrying bureaucracy a little too far. It seems to me that I should be charging for the service that I have been rendering his department, which will cost a good deal more in terms of saving time and money than what his department is charging me, $7 a month. One little vital piece of information that could be passed over my unit could save his department and the government thousands and thousands of dollars spent on searches.
If it is the intention of his department, or of CN Telecommunications, to insist upon a rental for my identifier to use CN-T facilities for telephone service, then I will discontinue the service, and I know of dozens of people like me who will do the same. Instead they will not carry CN identifiers; they will carry identifiers and communicate with mining companies and people in the air transport business that do not charge them for doing so.
Having said that, I do not expect any lengthy answers tonight, but generally speaking I think the minister's department is doing, apart from the few exceptions I have mentioned, an adequate job in the north. I extend to him a personal invitation as minister, having national responsibilities, to visit the Yukon and take a first hand look at the operations of his department there. I should like him to be my personal guest and I will show him things that I am sure will surprise him.

Madam Chairman, I thank the hon. gentleman for his last words. It does not happen very often that we in this chamber feel we are in a
Business of Supply
civilized world, so it was good to hear that. I would not cross the floor for it, but it was nice anyway.
I will not be able in two minutes to answer all the hon. member's questions. Some are a little too technical. I am not highly specialized in directional and non-directional beacons. I happen to know what they are, but I do not know enough about them to make a speech in the House and to say whether the hon. member is right or wrong. Perhaps tomorrow I can say something about that matter.
As far as an independent accident board is concerned, the hon. member is right. We are exercising pressure on the government House leader to bring in legislation as soon as possible to set up an impartial board that will inquire into causes of accidents. The accident he referred to indicates that we need an independent body, not because I think anything irregular happened but because at the time everyone felt a little uneasy. We will do what we can here in co-operation with the other House leaders.
As for the rate study, as the hon. member knows, it has been completed. We know it is feasible to have a railway going up the Mackenzie valley.
What about the one for the Yukon?

I understand that study is not yet completed. The other one is, but the one for the Yukon is on its way and is about to be completed.
With regard to the use of English and French, that is a debate in itself. It is too delicate a subject on which to throw out a few words just before ten o'clock. This would risk giving a false interpretation of what the hon. member said, or a false interpretation of what I think should happen in this regard.
If the hon. member does not mind, I will call it ten o'clock. I hope tomorrow to be in a position to answer the technical points he has raised.
