May 12, 1975
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: FISHERIES-EXCLUSION OF SOME AREAS OF NEWFOUNDLAND FROM COMPENSATION PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT ACTION
FISHERIES-EXCLUSION OF SOME AREAS OF NEWFOUNDLAND FROM COMPENSATION PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, may I say that the debate tonight is on a matter that I feel has been an exercise in dereliction of duty on the part of a federal-provincial committee appointed by both levels of government, that is, the federal Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland, to investigate the effects of ice damage on the west coast of Newfoundland in the year 1974 which destroyed many hundreds of lobster traps, and in turn resulted in the loss of livelihood for many hundreds of fishermen.
I would ask on behalf of these aggrieved fishermen how, in the name of fairness, the committee could declare certain zones on the west coast of Newfoundland which they determined should qualify, to the exclusion of other areas where it has become obvious that ice damage also existed, damage as serious in nature as that in those zones declared should qualify by the committee?
The damage existed along a coastline of some 300 to 400 miles in an almost straight line from Cape John in the southern part of the west coast to the most northerly part known as Cape Norman, yet that committee, in its questionable wisdom, declared an area almost half way between the two points, from Cape St. Gregory to Cape Norman; in other words, it declared an imaginary line which is not only questionable but smacks of discrimination against certain groups of fishermen. The committee acted as judge and jury without even the common courtesy of giving the said fishermen the opportunity to question that decision.
In the thrust of my effort to find out the basis for the declaration of the qualifying zones it has been impossible for me to get fair answers, beyond the normal bureaucratic answers from both levels of government that the decision was made by a federal-provincial committee. This is not good enough and is entirely unacceptable.
This unacceptability prompted me to investigate the ice conditions which existed during the 1974 lobster season from dates before, during, and well into the lobster season. I am satisfied as a result of Ministry of Transport reports, which I have today sent to the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc), that there is evidence which shows beyond a shadow of doubt that ice conditions in the excluded area were as fierce or, if not as fierce, were such that they warranted consideration for compensation which heretofore has been denied those fishermen in the Bay of Islands, Port au Port and Bay St. George areas.
I have at hand ice condition reports for 17 days, from April 16, 1974, four days before the April 20 lobster season opening, to May 14, some 28 days into the season, and during a period when the execution of the lobster fisheries is at its best.
Let me put on record just a few of these reports. On April 18, just two days before the season opened, there was close pack ice from Cape St. George along the west coast of Newloundland, which is right in the middle of the excluded zone. On April 22, the west coast of Newfoundland remained congested from Cape St. George northward, two days after the opening of the season and after the
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
laying of traps. On April 25 and 26, the report states that congestion of ice remained in the areas of Cape St. George, St. Georges Bay and Corner Brook. The report states that on April 29 there were strings and patches of ice in St. Georges Bay. On May 1 there was open pack ice in St. Georges Bay from Port au Port peninsula to Bay of Islands, on shore ice drift was increasing the ice concentration to open pack with a narrow strip of close pack ice across the entrance to the bay. On May 2 the report states that the west coast of Newfoundland remained heavily congested from Cape St. George, and with onshore winds this could cause some concern to west coast ports for the next week or ten days.
Finally, I will use only one more example of the report of May 10 which stated that open to very open pack ice was found north of the Port au Port peninsula extending 60 miles west of south head. The strait of Belle Isle was not recommended for commercial navigation at this time.
It is obvious then, Madam Speaker, that the reports from which I read substantiate the conditions which existed. They confirm that the committee was lax in its duty to declare the zones where damage occurred, and to support the requests of the fishermen in the area of concern. I hope the minister, who I know will be sympathetic, and his parliamentary secretary will review the reports that I have sent to him, and will cause a further investigation to be carried out and a review of the facts. If unfairness existed, I am sure he will not only rectify the situation but demand an ccounting by the committee to determine the reasons for their decision which is not helping the fast deteriorating fishing industry. I hope the anser will be satisfactory, both to me and to the fishermen in the areas concerned.

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Marchand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: FISHERIES-EXCLUSION OF SOME AREAS OF NEWFOUNDLAND FROM COMPENSATION PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member. He made his comments in a manner which, as usual, has been frank and informative. I think the hon. member made some new points tonight when he said that perhaps some errors have been overlooked by the provincial government and the federal government. I can assure him that the new information he has brought to the attention of the minister and the House tonight will be thoroughly investigated.
I know it has always been the position of the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) to be fair and just, and to do the right thing by the fishermen. That is the reputation he has gained so far as minister responsible for fisheries. I know he has been very co-operative in a number of ways and has tried to respond to the problems of fishermen.
However, I should say also that this disaster comes largely under provincial jurisdiction, a disaster which was declared as such by bhe province. The province must have made a request to the federal government for action, and we responded to the provincial request.
I should say in closing that we are always mindful of and willing to respond to provincial requests, but I hope we can take another look at this problem and perhaps we will find that some of the fishermen who have been left out should not have been left out of the program. We will really take another look at this.
May 12, 1975

subtopic: HEALTH-ASBESTOS LEVELS IN LAKE SUPERIOR-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO STOP ASBESTOS DISCHARGES AT SILVER BAY, MINNESOTA
HEALTH-ASBESTOS LEVELS IN LAKE SUPERIOR-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO STOP ASBESTOS DISCHARGES AT SILVER BAY, MINNESOTA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me apologize for not being here promptly at ten o'clock, but I was at a committee meeting. I can recall one time, when I was younger, driving home from Calgary to my home in High River listening to the radio and knowing where two different radio station outposts were. I was amazed that what I thought was the same man could be heard within instants on two different radio stations. I was not aware then that you could record and can announcements, as did that man. I cannot move as quickly as he did in getting from committee to the House, and I apologize for being late. I hope I did not cause too much concern in the House.
My question relates to a question raised on April 17 by me with the Acting Minister of the Environment or the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). I raise it again now in the adjournment debate not so much because of the substance of the reply but because of the attitude toward the House and toward serious questions on matters of human health and the environment which was displayed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in his answers.
My question was:
What immediate action are the federal officials taking to stop asbestos discharges at Silver Bay, Minnesota which it has recently been revealed are leading to asbestos levels in Lake Superior which are higher than allowable and which United States scientists consider to be dangerously high?
The Minister of National Health and Welfare replied that I should make my representations to my colleagues in the Ontario government, since the health aspect of water quality is controlled by provincial and municipal health departments in Canada.
What the minister did by that partisan answer was to try to avoid the clear responsibility which the Government of Canada had for asbestos discharges which occurred outside the jurisdiction of Ontario and outside the jurisdiction of Canada directly but within the jurisdiction of the International Joint Commission, and which were raising the prospects of very serious damage to human health in the Great Lakes region, and particularly in Lake Superior.
The escalation of reported concentrations of asbestos in Lake Superior has risen from a point where, three years ago, it was not considered to be dangerous to where, today, it is considered to be very dangerous to human health, according to the records we had in our hand when that exchange occurred here in the House of Commons. An International Joint Commission report filed in February of this year indicated that asbestos fibres from industrial sources were contaminating drinking water in communities in the whole Great Lakes basin, and indeed the report which prompted my question indicated that the estimates of the IJC study were very much less than the danger appeared to be from the concentrations which were found by qualified researchers in existence in Lake Superior. It was clear that there were dangers.
Adjournment Debate
It is acknowledged even by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in a letter to my colleague, the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick), that there is a danger of disabling but non malignant disease of the lung from asbestos concentrations. He went on to say:
It is also known that asbestos workers are more likely to die from cancers of the lung and gastro-intestinal tract than the average individual. More recently, mesothelioma, a relatively rare but highly malignant tumour of the pleural and peritoneal linings, has been strongly associated with exposure to asbestos.
Clearly there are some very real concentrations and possibilities of danger, and even lethal danger, to human health. It is not a matter to dismiss with partisan references or with directions to seek help in other jurisdictions, because there is clearly in the jurisdiction of the Government of Canada under the IJC generally a responsibility to care for the health of Canadians who might be affected by asbestos emanations.
I hope that in answering tonight the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Marc-hand)-and I know his minister was not in the House when the question was asked-will take this opportunity to outline the extent of action which the Government of Canada is now taking within its own clear jurisdiction to deal with harmful concentrations of asbestos in the whole of the Great Lakes basin.
This problem was pointed out three months ago by the International Joint Commission, and particularly in the area of Lake Superior, where it has been suggested by recognized and responsible experts that the concentrations might be lethally higher than that pointed out by the IJC study in February.
I hope the parliamentary secretary when he answers will also indicate what action the Government of Canada intends to take regarding the possibility of asbestos contamination in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada, and I hope that subsequently when matters of this kind, which relate directly to the jurisdiction of the Canadian government and directly to the health of individual Canadian citizens, are raised in the House of Commons, we will not be again exposed to a display of that kind of partisanship, and the attempt to hide behind provincial jurisdiction which was shown by the Minister of National Health and Welfare when this very important question was first raised on April 17.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hope the hon. member does not feel that I can answer all the questions he has raised in the three minutes allotted to me, but I would like to refer him to a statement I made on the same subject in response to a question raised by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae). I made the statement on April 29, 1975, that there are some conflicts with regard to both the type of fibres and the fibre counts in samples taken in Lake Superior by the different groups studying this problem, which have made the matter a little difficult.
At the present time the Canada Centre for Inland Waters at Burlington is co-operating with the Ontario ministry of environment to conduct inter laboratory comparisons of a common sample from the Thunder Bay municipal water supply. This sample is being split be-

May 12, 1975
Adjournment Debate
tween Canada Centre for Inland Waters, McMaster University, Ontario Research Foundation and Lakehead University. We anticipate this inter laboratory comparison will assist us in establishing norms for standardization of analysis, which has been part of our problem.
Many people in responsible positions have carried out studies on asbestos fibres. The Great Lakes Research Advisory Board of the IJC began preparing a summary report on the status of research investigations on asbestos in the Great Lakes, and particularly in Lake Superior, in March, 1974. The Department of the Environment was conducting studies to evaluate the possibility of transboundary movement of asbestos fibres in Lake Superior in 1973. McMaster University was also involved in studies in 1973. The Ontario Research Foundation and the Ontario department of the environment have also been carrying out studies of asbestos fibres. This research into the distribution of asbestos fibres has been ongoing and will continue to be so.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-SERVICE FOR SOUTHWESTERN MANITOBA AND SOUTHEASTERN SASKATCHEWAN-GOVERNMENT POSITION
AIR TRANSPORT-SERVICE FOR SOUTHWESTERN MANITOBA AND SOUTHEASTERN SASKATCHEWAN-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my comments are actually a continuation of our discussion on transportation. I am pleased to see the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mclsaac), who is also the member for Battleford-Kindersley, present as the subject I wish to raise tonight concerns his part of the country as well as my own.
My comments arise out of the question I put to the minister on April 30 with respect to an announcement that was promised by the minister on March 10 as being forthcoming by April 10 in regard to a study undertaken by Air Canada, at the request of the province of Saskatchewan for jet service into eastern Saskatchewan and western Manitoba.
Unfortunately the minister misunderstood the point I was making, and I think he replied to what he thought was a question on the experimental commuter service which is about to be launched into western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan. This is a service that will be sponsored by the Department of Transport in co-operation with the province of Manitoba. It is an experimental service of only two years duration and it is hard to fit it into any category that exists now with respect to announced air policy. It is not STOL and it does not seem to be third level air carrier service; it is an experimental commuter which will at least give some minimum air service in these important developing areas of Canada.
The point I wish to make is that this experimental commuter service will be just as ineffective as the other commuter services that have been tried in this area, such as the most recent one, the midwest service, which was withdrawn over a year ago, unless it is linked to a jet service which provides ready access to the rural parts of western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan, flying east and west.
In western Manitoba the airport located just north of the city of Brandon would be the centre of focus. Brandon is the second largest city in the province of Manitoba and

it has been without air service of any kind for over a year. It has a new air terminal all ready to go. I think that what has to be accomplished by the Department of Transport is a two pronged attack, a commuter service feeding into the Brandon airport, and connecting with an ongoing jet service that is now under study by Air Canada.
Perhaps when the parliamentary secretary replies he can indicate if the study has been completed, if Air Canada will be providing the service, and if Air Canada plans once more to resume regional area responsibilities. Originally Air Canada had this responsibility, but relinquished it to the designated air carrier, TransAir. Will such service, if assumed by Air Canada, be part of the service already available from Regina to Winnipeg, and to the east, with a stop-over at Brandon airport? Of course,, we shall want service in reverse order going west. It seems to me that such service, both east and west, is vitally important if the developing areas of Canada are to have the high quality of air service they need.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) covered two or three points in the question he raised this evening.
As the hon. member is no doubt well aware, the federal government has participated with the governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan in helping those two provinces set up a demonstration project with two Saunders ST 27 aircraft, to the tune of $2 million for the aircraft and another $1.35 million for the improvement of facilities at points those aircraft will serve.
The hon. member referred to the study being conducted by Air Canada with respect to air service in Saskatchewan. He made reference to this matter in an earlier question addressed to the minister. That study is the result of a statement made by the minister and, indeed, perhaps by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), during the last election campaign. The statement was to the effect that if provincial governments require the help of Air Canada and of the Ministry of Transport to look into particular air needs, help will be forthcoming. Following that, the government of Saskatchewan asked Air Canada to study its air requirements. It is my understanding that this study is not finished yet. Even though the Ministry of Transport is co-operating with Air Canada and the province of Saskatchewan, the study is being made at the request of the province, and it is up to the province to make the results public. I presume that perhaps it will.
So far as Air Canada providing jet service to the city of Brandon is concerned, I am not aware that Air Canada plans at this moment to provide this service at this point in time. I am not aware if the study being conducted by the government of Saskatchewan will include the possibii-ty of jet service per se to Brandon, but I am sure that it will be related to air service which will connect Brandon with that whole general area.
As the hon. member says quite rightly, the actual service being provided by this experimental commuter service does not seem to be a third level of service. Hopefully it will be a worth while experiment, will promote good air
